**Surah 27: An-Naml (The Ant)**

Its purpose is to describe this Book as sufficient for guiding all creation, by distinguishing the Straight Path (al-sirat al-mustaqim) from the way of those who are lost, and by gathering the foundations of the religion (usul al-din). This is because the one who sent it down has comprehensive knowledge of the hidden and the manifest. It also contains good tidings for the believers and warning for the disbelievers, concerning the Day on which the first and the last generations will be gathered. All of this returns to knowledge, which entails wisdom. So the greatest aim of this surah is to manifest knowledge and wisdom, just as the aim of the surah before it (al-Shu'ara') was to manifest force and vengeance. The clearest evidence for this aim is what the ant possesses of good management and sound methods of living, and especially what Allah, glorified is He, mentions of it concerning the soundness of intention in its governance, the excellence of its expression of that intention, and the eloquence of its conveying. [It begins with] "In the name of Allah" (Bismillah), whose knowledge is perfect so that His wisdom dazzles; "the All-Merciful" (al-Rahman), who encompasses all with guidance through the clearest exposition; "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahim), who bestows upon the one who keeps to the Straight Path the gardens of bliss.

﴿Ta, Sin﴾ indicates the purity of the Tur (Mount Sinai) and [the Valley of] Tuwa in it, the goodness of Taybah (Medina), and the blessing of Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House/Jerusalem) which Sulayman (Solomon) built, peace be upon him, [from which the forbidder of injustice went forth]. It also indicates that when Allah, glorified is He, purified the Children of Israel and made them good through trials, and they were patient, He delivered them from Pharaoh and his armies through the hearing of Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, of the revelation, which contradicts the poetry of poets and the lies and slander of sinners, from the Tur. (p-123) He did not mention the completion of their affair with the drowning of Pharaoh, because the aim of this surah is to manifest knowledge and wisdom, not force and vengeance. Therefore the situation did not require mentioning the letter Mim.

When he (al-Biqa'i) concluded the previous surah with the establishing of the matter of the Qur'an, that it is from Allah, and negated doubts about it and exposed the falsity of what they (the disbelievers) forced upon it by dividing their speech about it, saying that it was magic, confused dreams, fabrication, or poetry, all of which arose from the states of the devils, he began this surah by alluding to [the fact that it is] the eternal speech that is heard, purified of any blemish that could attach to it from any of that. Then he followed this by describing it as being, just as it is an ordered and gathered whole in wording and meaning, without any break or flaw, and without any defect or error. So it gathers the foundations of the religion and spreads out its branches, with what the existence of the Muslims alludes to. Thus He said: ﴿Those are the verses﴾ [i.e., the verses that are] of lofty station, far-reaching in aim, wondrous in arrangement, ﴿of the Qur'an﴾, i.e., the perfect in its being Qur'an, gathering the foundations, spreading the branches, which has no defect or break, nor split nor blemish, ﴿and a Book﴾ [i.e., the verses of] a Book, meaning: what a Book it is, which, along with gathering all that sets right the livelihood and the Hereafter, is decisive in its rulings and dominant in its rulings, in each of its untying and tying. Its being conjoined without following (i.e., the conjunction "and" rather than an appositive) indicates that it is perfect in both its being Qur'an and its being a Book. ﴿clear﴾, i.e., clear in itself that it is from Allah, [revealing] every difficulty, clarifying every obscurity, of the rulings and proofs regarding the foundations and the branches, the subtle points, the allusions and the knowledge, whether of what has been or what is to be. How wondrous is it as a gatherer that also distinguishes, a connector that also separates!

(p-124) Since the concern of this surah was more with spreading out (al-nashr), which is one of the necessary features of gathering in the root "q-r-a" (as its explanation has passed at the beginning of al-Hijr), he placed the Qur'an first. The evidence for this is the spreading out of the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, in most of his story: his separation from his mother, his departure from his homeland to Madyan, his return from what he had reached to what he had been in, his seeking for his family fire and guidance, the staff's transformation and the fear it spread, the sign of the hand, and all the nine signs, the choice of the expression "people" (qawm), whose original meaning is standing, the seeing of the signs, the spreading of the Hoopoe, the bringing out of the hidden thing (al-khab') from which came the teaching of the speech of birds, the speaking of the beast to people, the spreading of the woman [and] her people and her throne, after the messengers went back and forth between her and Sulayman, peace be upon him, the uncovering of the shin, the division of Thamud into two groups along with the dispersing dispute, the scattering of the people of Lut, peace be upon him, into what is not lawful, the dispersing of the winds as spreaders, the dividing of provision between heaven and earth, the passing of the mountains, and the spreading of the wind for the blowing of the Trumpet, from which arises the terror of creatures and the scattering of the graves, along with other things which, if you reflect upon the surah, its door will open for you and its veil will be lifted. This is in contrast to what is in al-Hijr, as has passed.

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When He made clear in Surah al-Shu'ara' the great mercy He showed through the Book, and the explanation of what it contains by which He exposed the enemies and showed mercy to the allies, and its being free from the devils ascending to it, and the striking signs that call whoever is guided by them to Him, its great signs made it distinct as a decisive criterion and a shining light, Allah, glorified is He, followed that with praise and commendation, and mentioned those whom His mercy encompassed by it, specially and with care, saying: ﴿Those are the verses of the Qur'an﴾, i.e., the verses resulting from these lights (p-125) ﴿of the Qur'an and a clear Book﴾ ﴿a guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾ (an-Naml: 2). Then He described them so that the follower may obtain his share of the blessing of following, and so that his hope of salvation may be strengthened from what He alluded to in ﴿And those who did wrong will know﴾ (ash-Shu'ara': 227), concerning the greatness of that outcome. Then He followed that with alerting to the description of those who are qualified for it, because of what preceded of false speech and fabrication, to purify His servants who are God-fearing and His sincere allies from the filth of doubts and disputation, and He said: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter – We have made their deeds appear attractive to them, so they wander blindly﴾ (an-Naml: 4), i.e., they are bewildered, not distinguishing between light and darkness, because of the confusion of thoughts and understandings. Then He followed that with consoling him, peace be upon him, with stories that occurred afterward, to energize him and to make known the loftiness of his station, and to inform him of the great craftsmanship of Allah, exalted is He, regarding those who came before. Then the surah concluded with the mention of the people of the Resurrection and some of what lies before it, and the allusion to the recompense and the salvation of the believers, and the warning to whoever turns away from his path, peace be upon him. – End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 2:

When He, glory be to Him, magnified the verses of the Book by what they contain of gathering together with dispersing, along with clarity, He mentioned its condition, saying: ﴿a guidance﴾. Since a thing may guide to an objective that troubles the state of the one seeking it, He said, negating that, and joined to it with the conjunction "and" (waw), indicating perfection in each of the two attributes: ﴿and good tidings﴾ [i.e., ] great ones.

When souls were eager and hearts were at ease, He withheld from those who are not worthy the great fruit of this, saying: ﴿for the believers﴾, i.e., those for whom this has become a constant attribute, owing to what they had before the summons of the caller, of purity of character and goodness of lineage. And in the explicit mention of this condition there is a hint that it is a trial and a warning to the disbelievers: ﴿He leads astray many by it and guides many by it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 7] – the verse,

﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, a guidance and a healing. And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is for them a blindness﴾ [Fussilat: 44], and other verses besides.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 3:

Since the attribute of faith is hidden, He described them by what attests to it of outward matters, saying: ﴿those who establish the prayer﴾, i.e., with all its outward and inward limits: its appointed times, the purifications, the conditions, the pillars, humility (khushu'), submission (khudu'), vigilant awareness of God (muraqabah), and excellence (ihsan), rectifying what is between them and the Creator.

Since the greatest purpose of zakah (obligatory almsgiving) is nothing other than providing ease for the poor, He said: ﴿and give zakah﴾, i.e., with excellence in what is between them and the creatures.

Since faith in the Resurrection (ba'th) is that which gathers this and other than it of all the acts of obedience, He mentioned it, magnifying it for its emphasis, saying, informing by making it a circumstance [illa] that it is a condition for what precedes it: ﴿and they﴾, i.e., while they, in fact, are.

Since faith in the Resurrection is the greatest cause of felicity and is the locus of wisdom, He expressed it with what implies exclusivity, not for exclusivity itself but to indicate the utmost firmness in faith in it, saying: ﴿in the Hereafter they﴾, i.e., those exclusively characterized by the fact that they ﴿are certain﴾, i.e., they bring about certainty (yaqin) in its true bringing-about and renew it at every moment (p-127) by what is brought forth from them of advancing to obedience and refraining from disobedience.

When al-Takhsis (restriction) implied that there are those who deny it, and its matter was firmly settled in human natures because of the dazzling proofs upon it in reason and transmitted revelation, the soul of the listener was eagerly drawn, out of wonder, to their condition. So He said, answering him, emphasizing with astonishment at those who deny that: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe﴾ i.e., who do not bring about faith and renew it, ﴿in the Hereafter﴾ — ﴿We have made attractive﴾ i.e., by Our majesty which cannot be repelled, ﴿for them their deeds﴾ i.e., the ugly ones, until they turned away from fear of their consequence despite the manifest ugliness of them. Attributing it to Him, glorified is He, is literal (haqiqi) according to the people of the Sunnah, because He is the true Originator, while attributing it to Satan is figurative (majaz) in the sense of causation. ﴿So they﴾ i.e., as a result of that, ﴿are in confusion﴾ i.e., they wander blindly like one who has no insight at all, and they hesitate and roam in the valleys of error, and persist in that, so at every moment they are in a new blundering, through an action that is neither right nor fortunate. For al-'Ama (confusion) is bewilderment and hesitation, as is the state of the one who has gone astray.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 5:

When He singled out the believers for what was known from Him, namely that they have a good reward and that in the Hereafter they are the successful ones, He mentioned what is specific to those (who are the opposite of that), so He said: ﴿Those are﴾, that is, the distant and the hateful, ﴿those for whom﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿is the evil of the punishment﴾ in both abodes: in this world, by captivity, killing and fear; ﴿and in the Hereafter they are﴾ (p-128) those specifically ﴿the greatest losers﴾, that is, the most lost of people, because they have lost what has no loss like it, namely their own souls, which they cannot replace.

When he had described the Qur'an as both a collection (al-jam') and a criterion (al-furqan), in a way that required explaining the people of success and the people of loss, and since the outcome of the disbelievers' condition is that they receive their disbelief, which is at the utmost of folly, either from the devils, who are at the utmost of evil, or from their fathers, who are at the utmost of [ignorance], he described the Prophet (ﷺ) with the opposite of their condition. He mentioned the greatness of the one to whom it was sent down and of the One who sent it down, so that it would be more likely to be accepted. He said, conjoining it to ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Naml: 4], ﴿And indeed, you﴾, meaning: and you are the most noble of creation, the most knowing, the most forbearing, and the most wise, ﴿are being made to receive the Qur'an﴾, meaning: you are made a recipient of it from the King. Here he omitted the intermediary and made the verb passive, to elevate him.

Since the matters that come from Allah are sometimes in accordance with wisdom, so they are attributed to their causes, and sometimes extraordinary, contrary to custom, so they are attributed to Him, glorified is He, and the extraordinary [sometimes] is at the first level of strangeness, for which the expression is ʿinda (with Him), and sometimes it is at its highest level, for which the expression is ladun (from Him), He, glorified is He, drew attention to the fact that this Qur'an is at the summit of strangeness among the kinds of extraordinary things, so He said: ﴿from One Who is Wise and All-Knowing﴾... [the text continues with the phrase] ﴿min ladun﴾.

When what had preceded at the end of al-Shu'ara' of the many wise purposes in its sending down in this tongue, and upon the heart of the master of the sons of 'Adnan, through the mediation of the Trustworthy Spirit, differing from the states of the devils, and other things that had passed, until it was concluded with a warning to the wrongdoers, (p-129) and the wrongdoer was more in need of wisdom than of mere knowledge, and he put first in this surah that it is guidance, and the guide is not followed nor is his guidance trusted unless he is wise in his knowledge, the context required placing the description of wisdom first, and the situation required the indefinite form for greater magnification, so he said: ﴿Wise﴾, meaning: reaching the utmost of wisdom, so none of His acts is except that it is at the utmost of perfection; ﴿All-Knowing﴾, meaning: of great knowledge, vast, complete, and all-encompassing. He is far removed from what they claimed about it, that it is the speech of created beings who have no knowledge or wisdom except what Allah has given them. The confirmation of this is the inability of all creation to produce anything like it, and to grasp some of its meanings as they truly should be grasped.

When He described it with complete wisdom and comprehensive knowledge, He indicated each of the two attributes, and the Qur'an's time and the greatness it has, which He alluded to at the beginning of the surah, through what follows in the surah of stories and other things. In this surah He limited Himself to these stories because of the great suitability between them and the purpose of the surah. He began with a story in which the distant people united in disbelief and were destroyed, while the close relatives in faith were saved. He followed it with a story in which the distant people were gathered in faith, and none of them remained behind. He made a third with another story in which a separation took place among close relatives, by the division of disbelief and faith. He concluded with a story in which distant people colluded in disobedience and persisted in disbelief, (p-130) so the earth swallowed them, then they were overwhelmed by water, just as the water reached the earlier peoples, and so there was a twisting in it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 7:

Since the connection of ﴿idh﴾ ("when") with the verb "remember" (udhkur) is so clear that it is hidden from no one, He said, indicating His wisdom and His knowledge: ﴿idh﴾ with its complement omitted, because its matter is evident, so it is as if He said: "Remember His wisdom and His knowledge when He said: ﴿Moses said to his family﴾ [i.e., his wife], while he was returning from Madyan to Egypt. It was said that she was the only one with him: ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾, i.e., I saw with a sight that brought me familiarity and removed from me loneliness and drowsiness, ﴿a fire﴾. Thus it is known, from what is in this story of decisive actions that point to complete knowledge, that He is described by the two attributes with observed knowledge. He placed [mā] first, for wisdom is more apparent in it, since the situation requires reassurance against lacking what he is commanded to do of actions.

Since it was as if it were said: "So what did you do?", he said, bringing the masculine plural pronoun to refer to the wife mentioned by the word "family" (ahl), which is suitable for the masculine and the plural, as a protection for her and a veil, and resolutely certain of the promise, by expressing with "good" which includes guidance and other things. So the attachment of hope to it was stronger than its attachment specifically to being guidance. And because the aim of the surah returns to knowledge, the firm certainty was most fitting for it; for this reason he described it as "the burning brand for those of understanding": ﴿I will bring you news from it﴾, i.e., with a true promise, even if I am delayed (p-131) ﴿from it with news﴾, i.e., perhaps some of it will be something by which we are guided to the path in this darkness, and they had lost their way. ﴿Or I will bring you a burning brand﴾, i.e., a flame of bright fire, ﴿a live coal﴾, i.e., a dry stick taken from the main part of the fire, so it is in a state where the fire has taken firm hold of it and so it will not go out. Al-Baghawi said: Some of them said: the shihab is a thing with light like a pillar, and the Arabs call every white thing with light a shihab, and the qabas is a piece of fire. The reading of the Kufans with tanwin is on the basis of apposition or description, and the reading of the others with the genitive construction, because qabas is more specific. He gave the reason for his coming with that, to convey that it was a cold night, by his saying: ﴿so that you may warm yourselves﴾, i.e., that you may be in the state of one who is hoped to warm himself by it, i.e., finds warmth by it, since the fire reaches him with me in it, and he indicated the nearness of his arrival, so he said.

﴿When he came to it﴾, i.e., that which he had supposed to be a fire.

Since clarification after ambiguity is greater, because of what it contains of arousing eagerness and preparing the mind to understand, he framed in the passive his saying: ﴿he was called﴾, i.e., from the side of God Most High.

Since the caller was left undefined, souls longed for his identification. Clarification by indication is greater, because it turns the soul toward inference. He (glory be to Him) drew attention to this by framing the speech in the manner of the speech of those who have power, to inform that He is the Supreme King. So he said, using the passive and introducing the explanatory particle, since the calling is in the sense of saying: (p-132) ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾, i.e., he was established in a firm establishment from which arises growth, purity and all goods beyond description. ﴿Whoever is in the fire﴾, i.e., its place, or its seeking, and this is a seeking in the sense of supplication. The expression indicates that the tree was large, and that when he drew near to it, the fire receded from him toward some of its sides [so he followed it, and when he reached the middle of the clearing, the light encompassed him]. The light was called fire according to what Musa (peace be upon him) supposed. [Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: rather, it was indeed a fire, as Musa (peace be upon him) saw it.] Fire is among the veils of God, as in the hadith: "His veil is fire; were He to uncover it, the glories of His face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reaches." ﴿And whoever is around it﴾, of all the angels (peace be upon them), and those holy lands [according to what God willed at that time and at other times]. It is fitting that those lands be as they are, because they are the place from which the prophets (peace be upon them) were sent, the descent-place of revelation upon them, and their gathering place for them, living and dead.

When the call came to him, as is reported, from all directions, so that he heard it with all his senses, he was commanded to declare God's transcendence, as a confirmation of a matter from His command (glory be to Him) and as a strengthening of it. So he said, conjoining to what the context guides one to estimate, such as: "so rejoice in this great good tidings": ﴿And glory be to God﴾, i.e., and declare the King, to whom belongs absolute perfection, to be transcendent in a manner (p-133) befitting His majesty. It may also be that it is a predicate conjoined to "blessed", [i.e.,] and God (glory be to Him) is exalted in a manner befitting His majesty above being in the place of the calling or any other places.

Since the attaching of this to the proper name indicates that He deserves it by the mere fact of His essence, which comprises all the attributes of perfection, of majesty and of beauty, He described Himself with what is known to be also deserved by His acts toward every creature, among which is what He wished to nurture in Musa (peace be upon him) when he was grown, after having nurtured him as a child. So He said: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾.

When the soul had longed to have the matter made plain, He said, magnifying Himself and paving the way for the dazzling miracles He wished to manifest through his hand: ﴿O Moses, indeed it﴾, that is, the matter, the great and sublime affair whose description cannot be reached, ﴿I am Allah﴾, that is, the One who has reached such greatness that imaginations fall short of it and the perceptive faculties of understanding are dwarfed before it. Then He made him understand, through what this contains, two attributes that indicate His actions toward him, so He said: ﴿the Almighty﴾, [that is,] the One who attains everything He wills, and nothing of what is with Him is reached except by the way He wills; ﴿the All-Wise﴾, that is, the One who undoes everything that another does if He wills, and no other can undo any of His acts.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 10:

Since the implied meaning (*al-taqdir*) is: "Do all that I command you, for it is necessary, and fear nothing, for no harm can reach you, because it is secured by the law of wisdom and guarded by the wall of might," this is indicated by the conjunction (*al-ʿatf*) in His words: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾. That is, so that you may know with the knowledge of witnessing (*ʿilman shuhudiyyan*) My might and My wisdom. Or it is coordinated with ﴿that blessed is﴾ [an-Naml 8]. So he threw it as he was commanded, and at once it became, by what the particle *fa* (then) indicates, a very great serpent. Despite its extreme size, it was in the utmost lightness and speed in its agitation when attempting what it intended. ﴿So when he saw it moving﴾, that is, quivering in its movement, despite its extreme bulk, ﴿as if it were a jann﴾, that is, a small serpent in its lightness and speed. This does not contradict its large body. ﴿He turned and fled﴾, that is, Moses, upon him be peace.

Since turning (*al-tawliyah*) in this case is shared among several meanings, he clarified the intended one with His words: ﴿retreating﴾, that is, he turned away fleeing from it, very swiftly, as indicated by His words: ﴿and did not look back﴾, that is, he did not return upon his heels, did not hesitate in earnestly fleeing, and did not look behind him after he turned away. It is said: *ʿaqqaba ʿalayhi taʿqiban*, meaning he returned. And *ʿaqqaba fi al-amr taʿqiban* means he persistently pursued the matter with diligence. This is in the ordering of the *Muhkam*. In the *al-Qamus* (the lexicon): *al-taʿqib* is turning around (*al-iltifat*). Al-Qazzaz said in his *Diwan*: *ʿaqqaba* means that he turned back returning, so he is *muʿaqqib*. (p. 135)

Since the soul was eager to know what was said to him in this state, it was answered: he was told, ﴿O Moses, do not fear﴾. Then he gave the reason for this prohibition in His words, giving good news of security and of the prophetic mission: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾, that is, in the place which is among the extraordinary breaches of customary norms (*nawaqid al-ʿadat*), namely the time and place of revelation. ﴿The messengers﴾, that is, because they are protected from injustice, and no one fears a just king except a wrongdoer.

When the beginning and end of the discourse both indicate that the intended meaning is what I have mentioned, and it is known from it that whoever does wrong fears, and since the messengers, indeed the prophets, are protected from committing wrongdoing, yet because of the elevation of their station and the greatness of their rank, what is less preferable (khilaf al-awla) is counted against them, and even some permissible acts that are equal in status, and more specifically, as they said: "The good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of those brought near (to God)," He, glorified is He, made an exception by the particle of exception to this, indicating what encourages those who are made to fear, regarding the consequences of wrongdoing, at the end of those (verses), in repentance. It also draws Moses, peace be upon him, to the forgiveness of his striking of the Copt, and that he has no fear because of it, even though his killing (of the Copt) was permissible since it was by mistake, although (the Copt) was a disbeliever. Yet the elevation of his station requires him to refrain from taking such action except with specific permission. For this reason he himself called it wrongdoing, saying: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [al-Qasas: 16]. This is among the allusions whose meaning is subtle. (p-136) So He said: ﴿Except﴾, or the meaning is: "But ﴿whoever does wrong﴾, whoever he may be, by an evil act, ﴿then substitutes﴾ through his repentance ﴿good after evil﴾, which is the wrongdoing he had committed. That is, the good is made to replace the evil, like the magicians who believed after that in Moses, peace and blessings be upon him. Then I shall forgive him, so that it is as though he had never committed it at all, and I shall show him mercy by bestowing upon him garments of honor that accompany security and might, even if he had earlier suffered some kind of fear. Then He gave the reason for this: that forgiveness and mercy are two attributes that belong to Him, so He said: ﴿Indeed I﴾ [i.e., I show him mercy because I] ﴿am Forgiving﴾, meaning: it is part of My nature that I erase sins with an erasure that removes all their traces; ﴿Merciful﴾, meaning: I treat the penitent among them with the treatment of one who is intensely merciful, by what his condition requires of honor, so I remove the effect of what he had fallen into of the cause of fear, which is wrongdoing.

And when Allah showed him this marvel in his hand—changing the substance of what was in his hand into the substance of another, animal substance—He showed him another sign in his very hand, by changing its accident (the attribute it had) into another, luminous accident. So He said: ﴿And put your hand into your bosom﴾, i.e., the opening of your garment, which is what was cut from it so that it may be stitched at your neck. ﴿It will come out﴾, i.e., when you take it out, ﴿white﴾, i.e., a great, exceedingly radiant whiteness (p-137), having a ray like the ray of the sun.

And since it might occur to the mind that this was a blemish, He said: ﴿without any harm﴾, i.e., without leprosy or any other affliction, as a sign ("in") among the ﴿nine signs﴾, as their explanation has already passed in the commentary on Surat al-Isra' and elsewhere, [these signs being] manifested through your hand, as My message to you ﴿to Pharaoh and his people﴾, i.e., those who are the most persistent people of this age in tyranny and transgression. Then He gave the reason for sending him to them with the marvels by His saying: ﴿Indeed, they were﴾, i.e., a state as if it were their innate nature, ﴿a people who defiantly disobey﴾, i.e., who go out of obedience to Us, so that You might bring them back to Us.

Since the sense was: "So he came to them as We had commanded, and they defied Our command," He said, drawing attention to this and indicating by the particle "fa" (then) the swiftness of his coming to them in compliance with what he had been commanded: ﴿So when Our signs came to them, visible﴾, i.e., through his hand, ﴿mubsira﴾, i.e., a cause of sight, because they were luminous and very evident. Thus they guide them to the straightest path as light guides the one who sees, so that it does not fail to show anything that ought to be benefited from. ﴿They said, "This is manifest magic"﴾, i.e., illusion with no reality to it, ﴿mubin﴾, i.e., clear in being an illusion.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 14:

﴿And they denied them﴾, i.e., they rejected them while knowing [the truth], ﴿by them﴾, i.e., they rejected that they were signs necessitating the truthfulness of [Moses], while knowing their [own] falsehood, because juhud (denial) is rejection along with knowledge.

Since jahd (denial) means rejecting a thing while knowing it, he confirmed this with His saying: ﴿and they were certain of them﴾, i.e., while the state was that they had sought to stand upon the realities of their matter (p-138) until they were certain of them as true, ﴿their souls﴾, and their knowledge of them permeated the marrow of their bones. Thus their tongues were contrary to what was in their hearts. For this reason, He attributed the certainty to the souls. Then He gave the reason for their denial and their description of them contrary to their [true] description, saying: ﴿wrongfully and arrogantly﴾, i.e., intending to place a thing in other than its rightful place, and being haughty toward the one who brought it, deceiving the servants of Allah.

Since the implied sense was: "So We drowned them all with the easiest effort and the least of matters, and none of them remained except a remnant, and no informant returned from them, despite their multitude, greatness, and strength," He followed this with a reminder of it, causing His saying to follow as a consequence of it: ﴿So look﴾. And He drew attention to the fact that their news is among matters that motives are strongly inclined to ask about because of its magnitude, so He said, expressing it with the interrogative particle: ﴿how was the end﴾, and the original wording would have been: "their end", i.e., the final outcome of their affair, but He made it apparent and said: ﴿of the corrupters﴾, so as to indicate [the] attribute that was the cause of their seizure, as a warning to everyone who commits the like of it.

When this story had completed the proof of His wisdom, the listener anticipated a proof of His knowledge, glorified is He. So He began with the particle of anticipation (ḥarf al-tawaqquʿ), indicating that there is no objection to the latter being superior to the former, and He conjoined it to what is implied in the sense: "Indeed We gave Musa (Moses) and his brother Harun (Aaron), peace be upon them both, wisdom, guidance, knowledge, victory over those who opposed them, and honour." (p-139) ﴿And indeed We gave﴾, i.e., with what We possess of greatness, ﴿Dawud (David) and Sulayman (Solomon)﴾, i.e., the son of Dawud. They were among the followers of Musa, peace be upon them, and came long after him by lengthy spans of time. ﴿Knowledge﴾, i.e., a great recompense of knowledge, including the speech of the birds and the animals and other things, which We did not give to anyone before them.

Since the implied sense was: "so they acted in accordance with its requirement," He conjoined to it His saying: ﴿And they both said﴾, thanking Him for it, indicating the nobility of knowledge and alerting its people to humility: ﴿All praise is for Allah﴾, i.e., the comprehensive attribution of all qualities of perfection, ﴿Allah﴾, i.e., He who has no equal, and to Him belong majesty and beauty, ﴿who has favoured us﴾, i.e., by what He has given us of that, ﴿over many of His believing servants﴾, i.e., those for whom faith has become a settled disposition.

(p-140) Since each of them, peace be upon them both, had been given what has been mentioned, he (the author) pointed to the excellence of Sulayman, peace be upon him, in that he combined with what Allah had granted him what He had bestowed on his father. So He said: ﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾, that is, from his father, peace be upon them both, to the exclusion of his brothers, in prophethood, knowledge, and kingship. Allah had singled him out, above his people, by joining kingship to prophethood for him. So he gave thanks to Allah for what He had bestowed on him, first and second. ﴿And he said﴾, that is, Sulayman, peace be upon him, relating the blessing of his Lord and drawing attention to what Allah had honoured him with, so that he would be more fitting for people to accept what he called them to of good: ﴿O people﴾.

(p-140) Since it is known that he had no teacher except Allah, and no one else could do such a thing, he said, building the verb in the passive (bani li-l-maf'ul, i.e., using the passive voice): ﴿We have been taught﴾, that is, I and my father, [with the easiest and simplest matter, from one who has no power over what we have learned. Had the intended meaning been him alone, there would be no grandiosity in it at all. Rather, it is the speech of one whose command is obeyed. This is a reminder of the greatness of Allah, through what He magnified him with, of matters that belong only to His power or to His command. This is as the Prophet (ﷺ) used to do when there was a situation requiring it, as he said concerning zakat: "Indeed, we will take it, and half of his wealth, as a binding command from the binding commands of our Lord, Mighty and Majestic." And as he used to write to some tyrants.] ﴿the speech of the birds﴾, that is, understanding what every bird intends when it makes a sound. Speech (mantiq) is what is vocalised, whether single or compound, meaningful or not meaningful. And it is no novelty that He who gave every soul its guidance, and taught it to distinguish its benefits and harms, gives it a faculty by which it perceives a mutual address among them, through which each kind makes itself understood concerning what it wants. This faculty falls short of human perception, because humans are particularly concerned with particulars arising from sensible things. ﴿And we have been given﴾ by Him who possesses greatness, with the easiest of His matters, ﴿of everything﴾, that is, that by which this is completed of the means of kingship, prophethood, and other things. He expressed it with the particle of totality (adat al-istighraq), magnifying the blessing, as one says of a man to whom people constantly come: "So-and-so is visited by everyone."

(p-141) Since this was a remarkable matter, he indicated it with his saying, emphasising it with kinds of emphasis, giving thanks, urging his own soul to more gratitude, and stirring it toward that: ﴿Indeed, this﴾, that is, what we have been given, ﴿is surely the manifest bounty﴾, that is, clear in itself to everyone who looks at it, making evident the high rank of its possessor and a unity that overflows with bestowal and giving.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 17:

Since this was merely a report, he followed it with what confirms it, saying: ﴿And there were gathered﴾, meaning: were assembled in a definite gathering, by compulsion, might and coercion, with the least effort, ﴿for Solomon, his hosts﴾

Since this indicated their greatness, he increased the indication of it with his saying: ﴿of the jinn﴾, beginning with them because of the difficulty of gathering them, ﴿and the humans﴾, mentioning them second because of their nobility and their sharing with them in that, in terms of the divergence of their aims and the dispersal of their intentions.

Since he mentioned those who have intellect and began with them because of their nobility, he followed them with what lacks intellect, saying: ﴿and the birds﴾. Since gathering (ḥashr) means assembling by force, and it is not free of dispersal, and the implied sense was: "He marched with them in some of the campaigns," he attached to it his saying, glorifying the army and its commander: ﴿then they were held back﴾, meaning: they were restrained, with an army whose first ranks are checked back upon its last, by the least command and the easiest of orders, so that they keep pace with one another. This makes for greater awe, more effective support in victory, and nearer safety. It is reported from Qatada that for every category of his troops there were wardens (wazaʿa, sing. wāzi‘) who turned back their first ranks upon their last, lest they advance ahead in the march. He said: "The wāzi‘ is the one who holds back, and he is the naqīb (officer in charge). The root of wazʿ (restraint) is holding back and preventing."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 18:

(p-142) Since the implied sense is "so they set out" (for the restraining of the troops can only happen while they are moving), he limited it with His words: ﴿until, when they came﴾, that is, they came up to [the valley]. And since he was on his carpet, above the back of the wind, between heaven and earth, he expressed it with the particle of elevation, saying: ﴿upon the valley of the ants﴾. It is a valley near al-Ta'if, as al-Baghawi transmitted it from Ka'b, and it is the one to which the soul inclines, for it is known up to now by this name among them. It is also called Nakhib (on the pattern of Wazn Kataf). I saw it when I set out for those lands to see their sites, to circle their places of worship and their haunts, and to seek blessing from the traces of the Guide, at the end and at the beginning. I stood at a mosque there near a lote tree called al-Sadira, which is well known among them as the place where the Prophet ﷺ prayed. This lote tree is mentioned in the account of the Battle of al-Ta'if in the Hishamiyya biography (al-Sira al-Hishamiyya). In naming the valley he restricted himself to Nakhib. I recited poetry there on the day I stood at its gate and humbly supplicated at its threshold:

"I passed by the Valley of the Ants, O friend, in the morning, so I cried out and let my tears run down my cheeks,

And I completed from it the standing place of the Hashimite, who filled the earth with tawhid, exceeding count.

And how many a standing place I spread out upon the free ground of my forehead, and displayed in its precincts the humility of the servant."

(p-143) In a long qasida.

Since they were in a matter whose sight is terrifying, and whose contact and experience weaken strength, the implied sense is: "then their vanguards appeared, their banners and glittering arms were seen, and their loads and baggage." With this he arranged His words: ﴿A certain ant said﴾, that is, one of the ants of that valley: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾. Since Allah, glorified is He, related of them what is the matter of rational beings, He used their pronouns, saying: ﴿enter﴾, that is, before the army I see arrives, ﴿your dwellings﴾. Then she gave the reason for her command, specifying its addressees, since its signs are not hidden. She said, as an answer to the command or as a substitute for it: ﴿lest Solomon and his hosts crush you﴾, that is, break you and grind you to pieces; that is, do not come out lest they crush you. This is a prohibition to them from coming out in the form of a prohibition to it, and it is more eloquent than stating their prohibition explicitly, because whoever forbids a great one from something has forbidden others from it even more strongly. ﴿Solomon and his hosts﴾, that is, for because of their multitude, when they enter the valley they rise over it and cover it, leaving no spot the size of a hand empty. ﴿And they do not perceive﴾, that is, Solomon, peace be upon him, and his hosts do not perceive that they are crushing you, being occupied with what they are in of the conditions of marching and attending to their affairs, along with the smallness of your bodies and your being hidden from the traveler in the state of your agitation and your staying. And her saying this indicates (p-144) her knowledge that, had they perceived them, they would not have harmed them, for they are the followers of a prophet, and so they are merciful.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 19:

Since this was a marvelous matter, given the eloquence of its words and the grandeur of its meanings, his saying follows from it: ﴿So he smiled﴾. Since this indicates laughter, and laughter may also come from anger, he emphasized it and confirmed its meaning by saying: ﴿laughing at her speech﴾, that is, at what she had been given of eloquence and clarity, and out of joy at what she described of justice, that he and his soldiers do not harm anyone while they are aware of it. ﴿And he said﴾, remembering what his Lord, glorified is He, had bestowed upon him through His good upbringing, from understanding her speech to other favors He had bestowed upon him: ﴿My Lord﴾, that is, O You who are good to me, ﴿enable me that﴾, that is, make me able to ﴿be thankful for Your favor﴾, that is, one who restrains it (wāzi'an lahu), holding it firmly and binding it, so that it does not overpower me, does not slip away from me, and does not stray from me for any time at all.

Since this made clear that the favor was connected to him [bihi], he confirmed it by saying: ﴿which You have bestowed upon me﴾. Perhaps his saying: ﴿and upon my parents﴾ implies that his mother [also] knew the speech of the birds. The verification of the meaning of this expression is that the root "w-z-‘" (wazaʿa), in whatever arrangement, revolves around the mi'waz (a worn rag in which a child is wrapped), and it entails distinction, for what is wrapped in it is distinguished from others. From it come al-awzāʿ (scattered groups) [p. 145], who are separated bands. It also entails capacity (iṭāqa), for most people find it; from it comes al-‘izūn (groups of people in a clan), for they are capable of what they wish, and those they wish are capable of them. From it also comes al-wazʿ, which is restraining what is to be restrained and being eager for what is to be increased, and from it comes al-ī‘āz, which is ordering the doing or forbidding. It also entails need, for no one is content with the old except one who is in need of the new. So the meaning of the verse is: make me one who restrains (wāzi'an), that is, able, to thank You for it, just as the one who restrains is able to hold back what he wishes to hold back. It is possible that the core of the root is need, because the awzāʿ, who are groups, need to gather together as a whole; the restrainer needs the one he restrains to comply with his command; the one who pulls needs restraint, that is, pulling; the one who is devoted to something is poor in need of it; and the one who admonishes needs his advice to be accepted. So the meaning is: make me wāzi‘an, that is, poor in need of gratitude, that is, constantly attached to it and devoted to it, because everyone poor in need of something strives hard to obtain it. This interpretation entails belittling one's own deeds, which becomes a cause of safety from self-admiration. [And in the verse there is an admonition regarding dutifulness to the two parents, in asking that they be given the ability to be thankful for what they themselves did not attain of gratitude.] And Allah is the Granter of success.

Shukr (gratitude) linguistically is an act that expresses the glorification of the benefactor because he is a benefactor, like praising the benefactor with what indicates that the grateful one has recognized his favor, acknowledged it to him, and that its place with him is good, and his heart has submitted to him for that. Its essence is that it is a name for knowing the favor, because it is the path to knowing the benefactor; for when one knows it, it causes him to come to know the Benefactor, so he takes the path of coming to know Him and strives in seeking, and whoever strives finds. It is narrated from Dawud, upon him be blessings and peace, that he said: "O Lord, how can I thank You when gratitude is itself another favor from You, for which I need yet another gratitude?" Then Allah, exalted, revealed to him: "O Dawud! When you know that whatever favor you have is from Me, then you have indeed thanked Me." Gratitude consists of three things. The first: knowing the favor, in the sense of bringing it to mind such that it is distinguished in your awareness as a favor. For many an ignorant person is treated kindly and favored while he does not know it, so gratitude from him is certainly not valid. The second: accepting the favor by receiving it from the benefactor, by displaying poverty and need, for that is a witness to accepting it in reality. The third: praising it, by describing the benefactor with generosity and bounty and the like, which indicates your good reception of it and your acknowledgment of the lowering of your rank relative to his, for the upper hand is better than the lower hand. It has three levels. The first: gratitude for the beloved things, that is, the things loved. This is a gratitude in which theists share: Muslims, Jews, Christians and Magians, for all of them believe that the kindness that reaches one from the Merciful must be recognized by the human being. From the vastness of the kindness of the Creator, glorified and exalted is He, is that He counted it as gratitude, although it is obligatory upon the thankful one, and promised increase because of it, and made reward for it obligatory, out of beneficence and kindness. The second: gratitude in adversities, which is either from a man who does not distinguish between states, but for whom the disliked and the beloved are equal; so when something disliked befalls him, he thanks Allah for it, meaning that he displays contentment with its descent upon him, and this is the station of contentment (riḍā). Or it is from a man [p. 147] who distinguishes between conditions; he does not love what is disliked nor is he content with its descent; so if something disliked befalls him, his gratitude for it is only the suppression of anger and the concealment of complaint, even if inwardly he is complaining; and the suppression is only for observing good manners by walking in the path of knowledge, for it commands the servant to be grateful in ease and in hardship. The third: that the servant witnesses none but the Benefactor, being preoccupied with immersion in witnessing Him so that he is oblivious to witnessing the favor. This witnessing has three kinds. One: that he be immersed in it through servitude, so that he witnesses Him as a slave witnesses his master with the courtesy of slaves when they are present before their master; they forget what they are in of rank and nearness that has not been attained by others, due to their immersion in courtesy and their attentiveness to their master, out of fear that he might come to them concerning some matter and find them heedless. This is a known matter among those who have associated with kings. So the possessor of this state, when his master bestows favor upon him in this condition, while he is standing in the reality of servitude, magnifies the kindness, because servitude obliges him to belittle himself. The second: that the master witnesses him with a witnessing of overwhelming love, so he causes this immersion in Him, finding sweet the harshness from Him. Some lovers of beauty of form, not the form of beauty, have said, and spoke well:

Whoever has not tasted the injustice of the beloved as its injustice, sweet, has ignored love and claimed it.

The third: that he witnesses a witnessing of unification which removes duality, annihilates the trace, and eliminates otherness, [p. 148] so when favor or hardship comes upon him, he is immersed in annihilation and perceives neither of them.

Since it is known from all of this that the grateful one is the one immersed in praising the benefactor by what is obligatory upon him of action, whether annihilation or otherwise, according to what he is able to do, and that such action may be something that could be an adornment for that servant, his being good, while he is not so, he said (ﷺ) indicating this meaning: ﴿and that I do righteous deeds﴾, that is, in reality. And since righteous deed may not please the benefactor because of a deficiency in the deed, as has been said regarding this meaning:

When the lover has little share, then his good deeds are nothing but sins.

He said: ﴿that pleases You﴾.

And since the pleasing righteous deed may not be raised to the level of those with whom Allah is pleased, because the doer is regarded with the eye of wrath, since he is one for whom the Book has preceded with wretchedness, because the bestowing King has perfect dominion and great possession, so He is such that He is not questioned about what He does, he said, turning away from his deed, acknowledging his inability, informing that the Benefactor is free of need of the deed and of anything else, that no disobedience harms Him and no obedience benefits Him: ﴿and admit me by Your mercy﴾, that is, not by my deed, ﴿among Your righteous servants﴾, that is, [for what] You intended them for of the completion of favor, by nearness and by looking upon them with the eye of pardon [p. 149] and mercy and contentment.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 20:

Since the implied sense is: he arrived at the station he intended, alighted there, and inspected the condition of his troops, as the care for the affairs of kingship requires, that is, he sought to avoid their loss by ascertaining who among them was present and who was absent, for it is incumbent that none of them be absent. ﴿And he inspected the birds﴾, since they were one of the pillars of his army, ﴿so he found the hoopoe missing﴾. ﴿He said: "What is the matter with me?"﴾, that is, "What has happened to me," in the state that ﴿I do not see the hoopoe﴾, that is, "Is it present, or has something concealed it from me?" And his saying, ﴿Or is he among the absent?﴾, just as it indicates what I have assumed, also indicates that he had lost a group of the troops, so he confirmed their absence and doubted his own absence. His mentioning the hoopoe alone, to the exclusion of them, indicates the great standing of the hoopoe with regard to the benefit it had for him, and that the absence of the others was by his command, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 21:

Then he said, by way of resumption (istinaf), establishing the policy of kingship, that which also indicates his greatness: They said: he sees the water in the earth as a person sees water from inside glass, so he strikes the earth and the devils come and extract it. ﴿Surely I will punish him﴾, i.e., because of his absence in what I did not permit him, ﴿with a severe punishment﴾, i.e., while keeping his soul alive, as discipline for him and a deterrent to his like. ﴿Or I will slaughter him﴾, i.e., as a lesson to others. ﴿Or he must bring me a clear authority﴾, i.e., one of these three things must happen; or the second "aw" (or) is in the sense of "illa an" (except that), so that the meaning becomes: one of two matters will certainly occur, punishment or slaughter, unless he brings me ﴿a manifest authority﴾, i.e., a clear proof for his excuse.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 22:

It is as if he said: "By God, he will certainly produce his excuse, or I will certainly do one of the two matters with him." ﴿So he tarried﴾, i.e., it followed from that that he remained, after the oath of threat, for a period ﴿not long﴾ from the time of the threat, coming out of fear of the awe of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and in fulfilment of what was incumbent upon him of service. [ʿĀṣim and Rawḥ, from Yaʿqub, read it with a fatḥah on the kāf (makatha), according to the more common pattern of past-tense verbs; the majority read it with a ḍammah (mukatha), indicating the intensity of his absence from Sulayman, peace be upon him, so that the vocalisation of the word matches the understanding conveyed by the structure of the speech.] ﴿Then he said﴾ [after his arrival, glorifying the matter, exalting the rank of knowledge, and repelling what he knew Sulayman had concealed of punishment for him:] ﴿I have encompassed﴾, i.e., in knowledge, ﴿what you have not encompassed﴾, i.e., you, due to the breadth of your knowledge and the extent of your dominion. Ihatah (encompassment) is knowledge of a thing from all its aspects. In this direct address there is an alert that the weakest of creatures may be given what the strongest cannot reach, so that the scholars may consider their knowledge insignificant and return knowledge of every thing to God. It also refutes the saying of the Rafidah: that the Imam is not hidden from anything, and that there is no one in his time more knowledgeable than him.

When he made it obscure to arouse curiosity and seized the heart's attention to learn of it, he followed with praise of the report, clarifying some of its obscurity, stirring the soul to seek its completion, and so he said: ﴿And I have come to you﴾, i.e., now, ﴿from Saba'﴾. It was said: it is the name of a man who became a designation for a tribe; and it was said: it is a land in the regions of Yemen. The wisdom of Qunbul's pausal pronunciation of it, with the intention of stopping, is to indicate the belittling of their affair in relation to the Prophet of God Sulayman, peace be upon him, that they have no movement at all with him, despite the grandeur, might and severe power they possess. ﴿With a report﴾, i.e., a great tidings, ﴿certain﴾. And this is among the most wondrous speech in its balance of wording and its harmony of script, together with its impressiveness and splendour.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 23:

So it was as if it was said: "What is it?" He said: ﴿Indeed, I found a woman﴾ — she is Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil — ﴿ruling over them﴾ [i.e., the people of Sheba].

Since she had been given of everything that kings need, a great deal, he said: ﴿And she has been given﴾ — he made the verb passive, acknowledging that she, despite her kingship, is one who is owned/subject (marbuwwah) — ﴿of everything﴾, to magnify what he saw of her affairs.

Since her throne — i.e., the couch on which she sits for judgment — was exceptionally great, he specified it by his saying: ﴿and she has a throne﴾, i.e., a couch on which she sits for judgment, ﴿great﴾, i.e., I have not seen the like of it for anyone.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 24:

Since she was among the people of that era closest to God in service, and so there had come to her a luminosity that made her dismayed at their turning away from God, she said, as a new statement expressing wonder: (p-152) ﴿I found her and her people﴾, meaning: all of them, [are] in great error. That is because they ﴿prostrate to the sun﴾, beginning that act ﴿instead of God﴾, meaning: [one who is] lower in rank than the rank of the Supreme King, who has no like, namely the rank of acts, since it is a created thing among His creations, exalted is He, whether that was with independence or with association. ﴿And Satan made their deeds appear fair to them﴾, meaning: this ugly act, until they came to think of it as good.

Since their being blinded from the path of truth resulted from that, He said: ﴿So he averted them from the way﴾, meaning: the way to God, for which there is no other way, which is what He sent His prophets and messengers with, peace be upon them.

Since their misguidance resulted from that, He said: "so they" meaning: in such a state that ﴿they are not guided﴾, meaning: there is no guidance found for them; rather, they are in pure misguidance and utter blindness.

When this misguidance was itself astonishing, let alone that it should come from a people united under a comprehensive kingship whose foundation is politics, whose seat is the intellect, which is the light of guidance and the remedy for error, he gave its cause as the absence of the greatest means of drawing near to God: prostration, magnifying it and exalting it. He said: ﴿Ala﴾ [i.e., because not] ﴿yasjudu﴾, meaning that this great blindness, by which Satan gained control over them, came about because they did not prostrate. It is also permissible for this to be connected to "adorned," meaning: he adorned for them [their deeds] so that they would not prostrate ﴿to God﴾, that is, worship Him to whom all perfection belongs, through prostration, which is the locus of intimacy, the place of nearness, the seat of intimate conversation, and the sign of well-being. For if they had prostrated to Him, glory be to Him, they would have been guided, since prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing. Thus Satan lost what he intended for them, namely misguidance.

According to the reading of al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far, with the lightened form and the prolonged fatha on the ya', this is a new sentence (isti'naf, a resumption of speech as an independent clause), begun with the interrogative particle as an alert to them of the magnitude of the matter, lest the admonition miss anyone among them by catching him heedless. Then he called out in the same manner and omitted the vocative, signalling that a gesture suffices because of the tightness of the situation, out of fear of hastening them to punishment before completing the phrase, which should have been: "Ala ya ha'ula'i usjudu lillah" (Unquestionably, O you people, prostrate to God), meaning: so that you may be freed from the captivity of Satan. For prostration is a means of pleasing the Merciful, a clarifier for recognition, and a fruit yielding the completeness of guidance and faith.

Since the story was concerned with explaining His, glory be to Him, knowledge, which precedes the knowledge of creation and entails wisdom, He described Himself with what implies this, saying: ﴿Who brings forth the hidden thing﴾. The hidden thing (khab') is that which is concealed, either actually, being hidden from creation in something else, such as the water within the earth, or potentially, being that which has not existed at all. He specified it by His saying ﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾ because these are the limit of our observation, so we see what comes into being in them after it did not exist: clouds, rain, plants, and what accompanies these, such as thunder, lightning, and others; what rises and sets of the stars; and beyond that the winds, cold and heat, motion and stillness, speech and silence, and what none can count but God, Exalted is He. The meaning is that He brings forth what is in the world of the unseen and places it in the world of the seen.

Since this may apply to what was not concealed in hearts, such as the water that the hoopoe used to bring forth, and since this may be known through signs, while what hearts conceal is more hidden, He said: ﴿and knows what you conceal﴾. Since this implies knowledge of what is openly declared, and since open declaration has an ability and tranquility that other things lack, though proclamation may contain clamour and the mingling of voices that prevents the listener from knowing, He said: ﴿and what you declare﴾, meaning: what they make manifest.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 26:

When this attribute necessitated that He alone be worshipped, He stated explicitly what it requires in His saying: ﴿Allah﴾, that is: the Supreme King, who has no equal (kufu'). [Since this was an indication that He has no namesake (samiy), he followed it with an explicit statement that He has no equal], so He said: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. And since the description of His Throne (arsh) as possessing some greatness, He said: ﴿Lord﴾, that is: the Originator (mubdi') and Manager (mudabbir) of ﴿the Mighty Throne﴾, that is: the one perfect in (p-155) greatness, to which no greatness comes close, and it encompasses all created beings (akwan). [It is established that its Lord is greater than it and greater than every great thing, by the verse of the Throne (ayat al-Kursi) and other evidence, so this cuts off the tongue of obstinacy at its mention, together with the greater demand of the context for it, because it pertains to the singling out of divinity (infirad bil-ilahiyya), which requires subjugation and majesty, unlike the verse of al-Mu'minun]. This is a verse of prostration (sajda) according to both readings, because the places of prostration are either praise for the one who performs it, or blame for the one who abandons it, as in the reading with the shadda, or a command to prostrate, as in the reading without it, [and all of them look to the majesty].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 27:

When his statement that this was a great report and a momentous matter was established, a longing arose for its answer, so it is said: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Sulayman, peace be upon him, said to the hoopoe: ﴿We shall see﴾, that is, we shall test what you have said, ﴿whether you have told the truth﴾, that is, in it, so that we may excuse you. And since lying in his presence, because of the greatness he had been given through prophethood and kingship, which no one after him possessed, indicates the firmness of one's foot in it, he said: ﴿Or were you﴾, that is, as a state akin to natural disposition, ﴿among the liars﴾, that is, known for being enrolled among them, [for in my presence none would dare to lie except one who is deeply rooted in lying], rather than "Or have you lied," because that could be a single occurrence.

Then he began with what would test him. He wrote a letter for him at once, in the greatest brevity, intending to hasten the removal of the wrong, on the assumption that the hoopoe was truthful, as far as he was able. He indicated his haste in writing it by his words in reply to him, ﴿Take this letter of mine﴾, which is the speech of one who had it ready with him and handed it over.

Since [Solomon], peace be upon him, had increased in anxiety because of their prostrating to other than God, he commanded him to hasten to the utmost. It is as though he was the swiftest of birds in flight, and God extended his speed beyond that, with help from Him, as an honour to His Prophet (ﷺ), so that he became like lightning. He indicated this by the particle ﻓ (fa) in His words ﴿then cast it﴾. Since [God] did not single him out in the letter from among them with a speech, so that their souls would be humbled before his address, along with what would show them His greatness, He used the plural and said ﴿to them﴾, that is, those whom you mentioned as worshipping the sun, and this is for the sake of giving importance to the matter of religion.

Since, if he had delayed from them after casting it, to a place where he would be safe for himself, given the speed he was in, they would have doubted that he was the one who had cast it, He commanded him to remain after casting it, hovering over their heads until they confirmed the matter. He, glory be to Him, indicated this by the particle of delay ﴿then﴾ in His words, that is, after your arrival and your casting, ﴿withdraw﴾, that is, move away ﴿from them﴾ to a place where you can hear their speech and they cannot reach you with it, ﴿and observe﴾ immediately upon your withdrawal ﴿what they return﴾, that is, what speech passes among them from one to another because of the letter.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 29:

Since the knowledge was established that he (Solomon) would certainly do what he was commanded, and that nothing would drive him except to the queen whose qualities he had described at length, the soul (nafs) yearned to hear her words at that point. It was as if it were said: "So he took the letter and went with it. When he delivered it to her and she read it, and she was a reader and writer from the people of Tubba' (the Himyarite kings), ﴿she said﴾ to her people, after she had gathered them, honoring them, or only their nobles: ﴿O chiefs﴾, that is, the nobles."

Since it is the custom of kings that no one reaches them with a letter or anything else except through the hands of their attendants, she magnified this letter by pointing out that it reached her by other than that usual way. So she used the passive form in her words: ﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me﴾, that is, by the delivery of a deliverer in a strange manner, ﴿a letter﴾, that is, a sheet in which is written a concise and comprehensive statement.

Since the noble person, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Ra'd, is one who conceals the bad qualities of character by displaying their good ones, because he is the opposite of the base person, and since this letter contained a dazzling nobility the like of which had not been known, both in terms of the sender, the messenger, and its opening with the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam, the Greatest Name of God), along with its brevity of wording and the reach of its meaning, she said: ﴿Noble﴾.

Then it [the letter] made clear its nobility, or it resumed with an answer to someone who asks: From whom is it, and what is it? So she said: ﴿Indeed it﴾, that is, the writing, ﴿is from Solomon﴾. In this there is [an indication] that beginning with the name of the author of a writing does not detract from beginning with praise. ﴿And indeed it﴾, that is, what is written in it, is: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. Thus He praised the One who deserves praise, the Supreme King, whose greatness encompasses the circles of majesty and generosity, whose mercy is general with every blessing. So the King of kings, from the abundance of the bounty He possesses, specifies after the general [bounty] whomever He wills with whatever He wills, of what His divinity is pleased with, from His general bounty. This follows the introduction of His name, as an indication that He is the One to whom worship is called, by what is due to Him in His essence and what He deserves by His attributes. All of this follows the introduction of the author of the writing, so that this would be more fitting for its acceptance, because most people only recognize the truth through men, and because of what the writing contains of indication to his prophethood. He explained his purpose with a compelling matter, so he said.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 31:

﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me﴾ meaning: do not refuse to answer my call or to submit to my command, as kings do; rather, abandon your haughtiness, since I am a caller to God, the One whom I have made known, in the "ba'" of the basmala, that no movement or stillness occurs except by Him, so submission to Him is obligatory, for He is the Lord of everything. ﴿And come to me in submission﴾ meaning: compliant and humbled, by what you have seen of my miracle concerning the matter of the Book.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 32:

When the soul (nafs) was eagerly awaiting their answer, the Exalted informed that they were dumbfounded, so He said: ﴿She said: "O chiefs (al-mala')!"﴾ Then she made clear what had entered her of terror from the owner of this book by her saying: ﴿"Advise me"﴾, meaning: be generous to me by making clear to me what I should do ﴿in my affair﴾ this, for which I must give an answer regarding this book. She made consultation a fatwa (legal opinion) in a broadened sense, because fatwa is the answer to an incident, and judging by what is correct is borrowed from fata (youth), in the age which is the choice of one's life. Then she gave the reason for her request to them by saying that it was always her custom to consult them on every weighty and trivial matter, so how much more on this grave affair. In this there is an appeal to their goodwill by exalting, honouring and esteeming them. So she said: ﴿"I would never decide an affair"﴾, meaning: in no circumstance would I be one who carries it out and settles it without hesitation ﴿"until you bear witness"﴾. This indicates the abundance of her intellect and the goodness of her manners, and for this reason her consultation of them in such matters bore the fruit of their obedience to her in ease and in hardship. Then the Exalted resumed reporting their answer with His saying:

"They said": that is, the chiefs, inclining toward war: "We are possessed of strength" — that is, in wealth and men — "and possessed of might" — that is, of resolve in war — "severe." "And the command" is referred back and entrusted "to you" — that is, both peace and confrontation are up to you. "So look" — because there is no dispute with you — "what you command" — that is, to do with it, for it will be heeded.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 34:

When she (Bilqis) knew that the one to whom the birds are subjected in this manner cannot be prevented from anything he wills, nor can anyone plot against him, she inclined toward peace. So Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, resumed the report about her with His saying: ﴿She said﴾, as a response to what she sensed in their reply of their inclination toward war, namely that the right course, beyond any doubt, is that we should devise a way to avert the intent of this obeyed king. Then she gave a reason for what the context of her speech made understood, with her saying: (p-160) ﴿Indeed, kings﴾, meaning in general, so how much more so this one whose command is executed and whose rank is great, ﴿when they enter a town﴾, meaning by force and conquest, ﴿they corrupt it﴾, meaning through plunder and destruction, ﴿and make the honored of its people humiliated﴾, meaning by the force they display against them and the tyranny they inflict upon them. Then she emphasized this meaning with her saying: ﴿And thus do they do﴾, meaning, and like this great-matter deed, whose path is difficult and whose reach is far, ﴿they do﴾ constantly; it is a habit of theirs, all of them persisting in this, so how much more so for one whom the birds, those that have nests, obey in whatever matters he wills.

When it had explained the danger in confrontation, she followed it with what she had resolved upon of peaceful dealing, and said: ﴿And indeed I am going to send them a gift﴾. Glorified is He, by using the plural in her words ﴿to them﴾ He indicated the greatness of what she was sending, namely to him and to his troops, ﴿a gift﴾, meaning one that would fall well with them. Al-Baghawi said: it is a gift given by way of conciliation.

﴿Then will I wait to see﴾ after that and because of it ﴿with what﴾, meaning with what matter ﴿the envoys will return﴾ with that gift from him, whether in words or in state, so that we may act afterward according to what we see of his affair, and thus we will have been spared the danger of advancing upon something whose outcome we did not know, and what we did will not have harmed us in any way.

The reason this is said: the intended sense is that she sent the gift. It is said that it consisted of five hundred beardless boys, whom she adorned in the dress of girls and ordered to speak in a feminine manner, and five hundred girls dressed in the garb of boys, whom she ordered to speak in a masculine manner. It also included a jasper (*jaz'ah*) with a crooked hole, an undrilled pearl [and other things], and she asked him to distinguish between the boys and the girls, to drill the pearl, and to thread a string through the crooked jasper. He ordered them to wash their faces and hands. A girl would take the water in one of her hands, transfer it to the other, then strike her face and pour the water over the inside of her forearm. A boy, as he took the water, would strike his face with it, pour the water over the back of his forearm, and let it run down over his hands. He ordered an ant (*al-arada*) to drill the pearl, and a worm to thread the silk through the crooked hole. Then he arranged, with the particle *fa'* indicating the speed of the sending, the words: ﴿So when he came﴾, that is, the messenger whom she had sent and dispatched. What is meant by "messenger" is a collective category. Abu Hayyan said: it applies to the plural and the singular, the masculine and the feminine.

﴿to Sulayman﴾, so he received that gift from them. ﴿He said﴾, that is, Sulayman, peace be upon him, said to the messenger and to those in his service, belittling what they brought: ﴿Would you provide me with wealth?﴾, that is, you and those with you and those who sent you. [My purpose toward you is only for the sake of religion,] belittling the matter of this world and making known that he has no inclination toward it in any way, and that nothing pleases him apart from obedience to God. Then he gave the reason for what made him regard what they had as trivial, saying: ﴿But what God has given me﴾, that is, the Supreme King who possesses all perfection, of wealth and majesty, through prophethood, kingship, and nearness to Him, glory be to Him. He is the One who makes His obedient servant independent of everything else, so whatever he asks of Him, He gives him. This is because He arrayed for him the jinn, humankind, the beasts of prey, the wild animals, the birds, and the creeping things in rows stretching for many farsakhs, and spread the whole place with pliant gold, among other things befitting him. ﴿is better than what He has given you﴾, that is, of [kingship] that has no prophethood in it and no support from God.

Since the intended sense is: "But you do not know that your gift is something one would be indifferent to, because you are bound to the outward aspect of the life of this world," he followed it with His words: ﴿Rather, you﴾, that is, through your ignorance of this, you magnify what you are engaged in, so you ﴿rejoice in your gift﴾, by supposing that the world will turn me away from you, because it is the ultimate goal of my aim. It is also permissible to mean that you rejoice in what is delivered to you, and thus abandon the one you wished to attack for the sake of what he has given you of worldly goods; so my state is the opposite of your state, for nothing pleases me except religion.

Then he addressed the Messenger in the singular, as a mark of respect for their leader, by saying: ﴿Return﴾. In his words ﴿to them﴾ he used the plural, to honour himself (the Queen's people being addressed through him) and to protect her name from being stated explicitly by her pronoun, and to generalise to everyone who concerns himself with her affairs and obeys her. ﴿Then we will surely come to them with hosts against which they have no power﴾, that is: no capacity ﴿to face them﴾, that is: to confront them in order to resist them and turn them away from their purpose; meaning, they are unable to oppose them. (p-163) ﴿And we will surely expel them from it﴾, that is: from their lands, ﴿humiliated﴾.

Since humiliation may be merely submission and not in the sense of disgrace, he clarified the intended meaning with his words ﴿and they will be debased﴾, that is: they will possess no strength of defence if they do not acknowledge Islam.

He said, when the messengers had departed and he (ﷺ) knew, from what he saw of their humility before his awe and majesty, which his Lord had bestowed upon him, and from his greatness, that they would come to him in submission. He said to his assembly, confirming his statement: ﴿And we have been given of everything﴾ [an-Naml 27:16], to inform them that she had made her throne secure: ﴿O assembly! Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ That is, the nobles. ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne﴾, so that she may see some of the extraordinary signs that God has given me, and so that she will be more ready to follow me in religion, and so that I may take it before its lawful taking becomes unlawful through her acceptance of Islam, and so that I may test her intellect. ﴿Before they come to me﴾ [that is:] she and her people ﴿in submission﴾, that is, yielding to my authority, abandoning the glory of their rule, and stripped of their great station, so that this will be more effective in establishing the proof (hujjah) against her concerning my prophethood, and more conducive to the firm establishment of faith in her heart and her sincerity in it.

"An ʿifrīt (a powerful jinn) said," and since this word is applied to the lion, to the strong rebellious jinn (mārid), to the man who is effective in a matter and exaggerates it with cunning and strength, and al-Rāzī said: "with malice and deceit," and to others besides, he clarified it by saying: ﴿I am from the jinn﴾, the cunning one, the harsh and mighty, ﴿I will bring it to you﴾. Since he knew that his aim was speed, he said: ﴿before you rise from your place﴾, that is, this assembly of yours. Then he affirmed and emphasized the matter by saying: ﴿And indeed I am strong for it﴾, that is, for bringing it safely, ﴿trustworthy﴾, one whose inability in it is not feared and from whom no diminishing of any part of it is feared.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 27, verse 40:

Since the story was told to display the excellence of knowledge, which entails wisdom, as evidence that He, may He be exalted, is All-Wise and All-Knowing, and to encourage the Qur'an and urge adherence to the clarity it provides, He said, relating this as a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*) in answer to the Prophet's (ﷺ) longing for something closer to that: ﴿One who had knowledge of the Book said﴾.

Since the Books of God possess a greatness that none but God can encompass, He indicated this by leaving the word for "what" indefinite in reference to this one who performs such a great marvel from it, so He said: ﴿knowledge﴾ [alerting that he was empowered to do that by the strength of knowledge, so that this would convey the glorification of knowledge and the urging to seek it, and He clarified that this excellence belongs only to the religious knowledge, so He said]: ﴿of the Book﴾, that is, the one [which is in reality the only Book, the one ascribed to us, and it seems to be the one] that was famous in that era.
