It may be the Torah and the Psalms, indicating that whoever serves a Book with the right service (p-165) is, as has come in our law, God, may He be exalted, his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he seizes, and his foot with which he walks. That is, He does for him whatever he wills. It was said regarding his identity that he was Asaf ibn Barkhiya, and he was a truthful, learned man: ﴿I will bring it to you﴾. This is more evident in it being an active participle (*ism fa'il*), since the act accompanied the speech. He showed his superiority over the ʿifrīt by His saying: ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾ [that is, comes back] ﴿to you﴾, that is, your gaze, when you blink with your eyelids and send it to its furthest point and then bring it back. Al-Qazzaz said: *ṭarf al-ʿayn* is the extension of the eye's gaze as far as it reaches, and for this reason they say: "I will not do that as long as my *ṭarf* returns to me," meaning as long as I can see. It is also said: *al-ṭarf* is a term for the collective gaze, not dualized nor pluralized. He clarified the confirmation of his act by His saying that he had taken control of it before the ʿifrīt could gain authority over it, so the glance hastened to bring it, as His statement, may He be exalted, indicates: ﴿Then when he saw it﴾, that is, the throne.

Since seeing may be at a distance and figurative, and likewise being "with" (*ʿindiyya*), He clarified that it was real by making explicit the governing verb of the adverbial complement (*ẓarf*), which in other contexts ought to be omitted, so He said: ﴿established near him﴾, that is, firmly fixed, with a stability that admits no doubt, not sorcery, nor a dream, nor an image. The Imam Jamal al-Din ibn Hisham said in the third chapter of his book *al-Mughni*: Ibn ʿAtiyya claimed that *mustaqirran* (established) is the dependent element that is assumed in such instances, and that is clear. The correct view is what Abu al-Baqa' and others said, that this *istiqrar* means the absence of movement, not mere existence and occurrence, so it is a specific state.

﴿He said﴾, that is, Sulayman, peace be upon him, out of gratitude for what God gave him of these marvels: ﴿This﴾, that is, this definite arrival, ﴿is from the bounty of my Lord﴾, that is, who has done good to me, not by any deed for which I deserve anything, for He has done good to me by bringing me out of non-existence and enabling me to act. Thus every act is a blessing from Him, which obliges me to give thanks for it. For this reason He said: ﴿that He may test me﴾, that is, He deals with me as one who tests and observes, ﴿whether I am grateful﴾, acknowledging that it is a bounty, ﴿or ungrateful﴾, thinking that I received it by merit. Then he increased the urging of his own soul to gratitude by His saying: ﴿And whoever is grateful﴾, that is, performs gratitude to his Lord, ﴿is only grateful for his own self﴾, for its benefit returns to it. As for God, He is too exalted to have any benefit from anything or any harm upon Him from it. ﴿And whoever is ungrateful, then indeed my Lord﴾, that is, the one who does good to me by granting me success in what I am in of gratitude, ﴿is Self-Sufficient﴾, that is, free of gratitude, whose not being given does not harm Him at all, ﴿Most Generous﴾, who deals with him by pouring blessings upon him, as one who shows his good qualities and conceals his faults. [Then He is worthy of cutting off His kindness if he persists in his sin, as the wealthy person does with one who persists in denying his kindness, and then he is destroyed] (p-167).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 41:

When he (Sulayman) had put first the gratitude, as is the custom of the righteous, and knew that she (the queen) would do with the throne what he had brought it for, her soul yearned for it, and it was answered by his saying: ﴿He said﴾ [i.e.,] Sulayman, peace be upon him: ﴿Disguise her throne for her﴾, i.e., by altering some of its features and its form, as a test of her intellect, just as she had tested us with the young boys and the young girls, the pearl, and other things. To this is the allusion in his saying: ﴿We shall see whether she is guided﴾, i.e., to knowing it, so that this would be a cause of her being guided in the religion ﴿or whether she is among those who are not guided﴾, whose condition is that they ﴿are not guided﴾, i.e., rather they are in the utmost of heedlessness, no guidance renews for them, and indeed if they were guided they would stop at doubts, dispute with falsehood, and would not reach a resolution.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 42:

And he indicated the speed of her coming, as a sign of her submission, by using the particle *fa'* (expressing immediate sequence) in His words: ﴿When she came﴾. Her coming, as it is said, was with twelve thousand *qayls* (tribal chiefs, sing. *qayl*) from the regions of Yemen, under the command of each *qayl* were many thousands. She had placed her throne inside a well-fortified palace and had assigned to it fierce guards. ﴿It was said﴾, that is, to her, when she saw her throne after it had been disguised, its appearance altered and changed. It was said by one who could not refrain from asking her a question, because of the awe that had come upon her and the terror that mingled with her at the great things she had seen. He addressed her with a single word that contains four words: the *ha'* of alerting (*ha' al-tanbih*), the *ka'* of comparison (*kaf al-tashbih*), the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishara*), and it is introduced by the interrogative *hamza* (*hamzat al-istifham*), meaning: "Pay attention!"

﴿Is this like your throne?﴾ Is it similar to this throne? ﴿She said﴾, turning away from the proper answer of "yes" or "no", as a sign that what was more likely in her opinion was that it was indeed the very same one, just as they say in "*ka'anna Zaydan qa'im*" (it is as if Zayd is standing): ﴿It is as if it were it﴾. This indicates great steadiness, a penetrating mind, a firm insight, and a receptive disposition, in accepting the possibility of miracles and submitting to them, despite the amazement of her arrival and the preoccupation of her mind with what had overwhelmed her of his awe and the magnitude of his affair. Sulayman, peace be upon him, [knew her soundness of mind and the falsehood of what the devils had said about his deficiency, fearing that he might marry her and that she would then reveal to him the secrets of the jinn, because her mother had been a jinn], as it is said. And they said that her leg was like the hoof of a donkey, and that she had very abundant hair.

Although she was nonetheless confused about it and did not reach the full certainty of its unveiling, even though she had been overcome regarding her throne while it was under guard, (ﷺ) recalled what Allah had specifically given him of knowledge, to increase his encouragement to gratitude. So he said, conjoining it to what is implied: ﴿We were given the knowledge﴾ before her, which implies: "She was given knowledge about the matter of her throne," but she has doubt gnawing at her; this shows that she was, in general, among the people of knowledge who are prepared for guidance. Or the implied meaning, according to what is indicated by what necessarily follows from her words "as if it were it," is: she was ignorant of the matter of her throne despite her great familiarity with it. ﴿And we were given﴾, expressing it with the *nun* of the one whose command is obeyed, especially since what is given is a cause of legal eminence, namely the knowledge which no one but Allah can bestow. For this reason the verb was put into the passive voice, because its agent is known. ﴿The knowledge﴾, that is, with all the knowledge that Allah has given us, among which is that this (matter) is hidden from her ﴿before her﴾, that is, before her coming, that her throne would be confused for her; or before her knowledge of what she supposed about the matter of her throne; or, "I and my predecessors existed before her existence, so we are deeply rooted in knowledge, and therefore we are upon certainty in all our affairs." He said, ﴿We shall see whether you are guided﴾ [an-Naml: 41] only in relation to his soldiers.

Then he mentioned the cause of the existence of this knowledge, its extent and its stability, and said: ﴿And we have been﴾, that is, together with the knowledge for which Allah prepared us by placing in our natures the luminous quality ﴿Muslims﴾, that is, submitting to Allah, Exalted, firmly established in that, turning fully to all His commands in action, according to His command, as indicated by His saying, Exalted: ﴿Fear Allah, and Allah teaches you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282] ﴿Their Lord guides them by their faith﴾ [Yunus: 9].

Since the meaning was: "As for her, although she had been given knowledge, it was not firm, and there was no religion with it," he expressed this with his saying: ﴿And what she used to worship besides God turned her away﴾. That is, it turned her away from the perfection of knowledge (p-170), just as it turned her away from religion. The "ما" (*mā*, "what") refers to the object of worship, ﴿she used to worship﴾, meaning a state firmly established in the past, ﴿worship﴾, meaning worship that had begun, ﴿besides God﴾, meaning other than the Supreme King, who possesses all perfection, or the lowest of the ranks of His rank. This was the worship of the sun, so that the distinction would become apparent between the party of God, the Wise, the All-Knowing, and the party of Iblis, the foolish and ignorant. Then he gave the reason for this, pointing to the great blessing of God upon her by the blessing upon her forebears, with his saying: ﴿Indeed she was from a people﴾, meaning possessors of might and power, ﴿disbelievers﴾. The word "إنّها" (*innahā*, "indeed she") was also read with a fatḥah on the *alif* (*annahā*), as a *badal* (substitute, or apposition, a grammatical replacement) for the *fāʿil* (grammatical subject) of "صَدَّ" (*ṣadda*, "turned away"). That was the cause, even though she was at the height of abundance of intellect, clarity of mind, and receptivity to knowledge, as her reflection concerning her throne indicates, "and none is guided to this except one who has the capacity for guidance". By her following their footsteps in religion, the mirror of her thought became rusted, and the swords of her intellect grew dull.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 44:

When this was complete, it was as if it were said: "Was there, after that, a test?" It was said: "Yes!" ﴿It was said to her﴾ [i.e.,] by a speaker from among the soldiers of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and opposing it was not possible for her because of the awe there of kingship, prophethood and religion: ﴿Enter the palace (sarh)﴾ [which is a palace] that he had built before her arrival, and he sat at its front, and made its courtyard of clear white glass, and let water flow beneath it, and placed in it the creatures of the sea. Its root meaning, as he said in the Jam' bayn al-'Subab wal-Muhkam: a single building erected standing alone, huge and tall in the sky. He said: It was said: every spacious, elevated building; and it was said: it is the palace; and it was said: every high, elevated building. And al-sarh: smooth ground, and sarhat al-dar is its courtyard. He indicated her hastening to comply with the command [and the speed of her entry] by the particle fa', so he said: ﴿So when she saw it﴾. And he expressed it with what belongs to supposition, indicating that her intellect, although in the utmost soundness, was deficient because she worshipped other than God, so he said: ﴿she supposed it﴾, i.e., because of the great clarity of the glass and the joining of the water to its lower surface, ﴿to be a pool (lujjah)﴾, i.e., a great expanse of water, so she resolved to wade through it, showing complete submission, ﴿and she uncovered her shins﴾, i.e., so that her garments would not get wet and she would need to change them before reaching Sulayman, peace be upon him. So he saw her as the most beautiful of people in shin and foot, except that she was hairy.

When his purpose was achieved, the report about his affair after that was resumed, so it was said: ﴿He said﴾, clarifying the greatness of his intellect and knowledge, his wisdom and power, and emphasizing that, because of the intensity of its resemblance to the excellence of the material and the extreme beauty and perfection of its craftsmanship, it hardly seems believable that it is a barrier before the water: ﴿Indeed, it﴾, i.e., this which you supposed to be water, ﴿is a palace (sarh) made smooth (mumarrad)﴾, i.e., polished, and the root of marradah is smoothness and evenness ﴿of﴾, i.e., made of ﴿glass (qawarir)﴾, i.e., crystal, so that it has the quality of transparency like water, and so one supposes there is no barrier before it. When she saw what God had favored him with of knowledge, supported by wisdom, completed by dignity and tranquility, perfected by extraordinary signs, she hastened to obey him, knowing that he was the Messenger of God. Then God, exalted, resumed the report about that with His saying: ﴿She said﴾, turning toward the one who had come to her, seeking rain from His bounty and asking for His great downpour: ﴿My Lord﴾, i.e., O You who are good to me, ﴿indeed I have wronged myself﴾, i.e., by what I was in of blindness, worshipping other than You instead of Your worship, ﴿and I have submitted﴾, i.e., so that the fruits of Islam may appear upon me.

When she mentioned this foundation, without which no obedience can be validly built, she followed it with the caller, without whom the fruits of deeds founded upon it are not complete except through love for him, submission to him, obedience to him and acknowledgment of his favor, and through his guidance to what is suitable of them and what is not, in the forms which cannot stand except by them, in quantities and qualities. So she said: ﴿with Sulayman﴾.

When she mentioned the attribute of lordship which requires worship through beneficence, she mentioned the greatest Name, which indicates the Essence possessing the attributes that require divinity [for the Essence], so she said: ﴿for God﴾, i.e., acknowledging Him as deity and lord in the manner of oneness. Then she returned, [indicating] the inability to know the Essence in its true knowing, to the acts which are the sea of knowledge, so she said: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. She generalized after having particularized, indicating the ascent from the lowest depths of blindness to the highest degrees of guidance. So by God, how wise she was! How good and noble was her lineage! It is said that Sulayman, peace be upon him, married her and made the bath (hammam) — and he was the first to make it — and removed her hair with depilatory (nawrah).

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 45:

When Allah, glorified is He, completed this story, which is founded on knowledge, built upon wisdom, and which indicates that the people addressed in it unanimously submitted to entering Islam despite their disdain for the kingdom and the dignity of their leadership, and despite being subdued at the hand of a stranger, far removed from them, He followed it with a story whose people divided into two groups, in humiliation and poverty, even though the one calling them does not remove any of their honor by following him. This is in addition to the wisdom it contains and its display of subtle knowledge in nullifying scheming after a long period of patience and forbearance. Exalted is He, He said, opening with the particle of expectation and affirmation for those who thought that this was the custom of every messenger with the people he calls, conjoining it to ﴿And We had certainly given David﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 15]: ﴿And We had certainly sent﴾, that is, with what We possess of greatness, ﴿to Thamud﴾. Then He pointed to the wonder of their hesitation by His saying: ﴿their brother Salih﴾, thereby combining in him the goodness of deed, the goodness of name, and the nearness of lineage.

Then He mentioned the purpose of the message in the most just and most excellent manner, which is acknowledging the truth to its people. (p-174) So He said: ﴿Worship Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King [who has no equal] alone, ﴿and do not associate anything with Him﴾, especially anything that neither harms in any way nor benefits, as an explanation that the messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, agree upon this, both Arabs and non-Arabs.

Then He increased the wonder at them by what the fa' (فَ) and the particle of suddenness (إذا) indicate of the haste toward separation with what calls to unity, so He said: ﴿Then suddenly they﴾, that is, Thamud, ﴿were two factions﴾. Then He clarified by His saying: ﴿disputing﴾ that it was a division of separation through disbelief and faith, not a division of unity in guidance and recognition. So some of them affirmed Salih and followed him, as has passed in al-A'raf. The indication to this comes here in His saying: ﴿and those with you﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 47]. And some of them persisted in their polytheism and their lying, and each faction says: "I am upon the truth, and my opponent is upon falsehood."

Then he resumed with what the particle of expectation (harf al-tawaqqu') indicated of intense longing, saying: ﴿He said﴾, i.e., Salih, seeking their compassion for their guidance: ﴿O my people﴾, i.e., O sons of my paternal uncle and whoever among them is sufficient to undertake the affairs of the community; ﴿why do you seek to hasten﴾, i.e., you seek to hasten [the coming of] ﴿the evil﴾, i.e., the state whose harm is certain, which is the punishment with which I warned those who disbelieved; ﴿before﴾ ﴿the good﴾, i.e., the good things with which I give you glad tidings in this world and the Hereafter if you believe. Hastening (al-isti'jal) is seeking the occurrence of a matter before its appointed time (al-waqt al-madrub lahu), and their hastening for this was out of persistence in its cause and their saying in mockery: ﴿Bring us what you threaten us with﴾ [al-A'raf: 77]. ﴿Why not﴾, i.e., would that you, why do you not, ﴿seek forgiveness from Allah﴾, i.e., seek the forgiveness of the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, for your past sins, by returning to Him in repentance and sincerely devoting worship to Him; ﴿perhaps you will be shown mercy﴾, i.e., so that you may be hopeful that you will be treated by everyone who has goodness [with the treatment of one who is shown mercy], by being given good and protected from harm.

Then he resumed relating their reply, saying: ﴿They said﴾, with harshness and severity, the doubling (idgham, the assimilation of two identical consonants) indicating that what they were saying is only understood by the adept (al-huzzaq) who know the science of omen-reading (al-zajr), [although the apparent meaning is the opposite, namely what he brought them of the she-camel, whose existence contained great blessing]: ﴿We have taken an omen from you﴾, that is, we consider you a bad omen, ﴿and from those who are with you﴾, that is, those who believe in you. For discord has arisen between us because of you, much talk and gossip and rumor have multiplied, and hardships and oppression have befallen us, because we have made you like the bird that passes from the direction of the north, as will come in Surat al-Saffat. ﴿He said: Your omen﴾, that is, what you take as auspicious, which yields what pleases you, or what you consider inauspicious, which produces what displeases you, and it is your deeds, good or evil, ﴿is with God﴾, that is, with the Supreme King who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, and nothing of it is in the hand of another, nor is it attributed to Him [so if He wills He makes us its cause, and if He wills He makes others its cause]. (p-176) Since the meaning of attributing it to God is that this evil which is upon you now is not from us, He said: ﴿Rather you are a people being tried﴾, that is, you are being tested by the Most High King through what you attribute to the bird of good and evil, meaning you are being dealt with by way of testing: whether you are fit for good by turning back from sin, so that it will be lightened for you, or not, and then you will be afflicted.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 48:

When he had informed about the majority of this group with evil, he informed about their evil through his saying: ﴿And there were in the city﴾, that is, in their city al-Hijr, among the leading men (ʿuzamaʾ) and notables (aʿyan) of the town, ﴿nine men (tisʿatu rahṭin)﴾, that is, men, corresponding to the nine signs (āyāt) of Moses.

Since al-Rahṭ (lit. "a group of men," the band of one's kin and supporters) carries the meaning of "people" and "men," the number nine was attributed to it, so it is as if it were said: nine men. Although it refers to a specific group of men, namely those numbering between three or seven [up to ten], and what is fewer than nine is a nafar (a small company). Al-Fayruzabadi said in al-Qamus that al-nafar is what is fewer than ten, except that it conveys dispersal, whereas al-rahṭ conveys greatness, strength, and cohesion. ﴿They were corrupting﴾, and he said: ﴿in the land﴾, as an indication of the generality and continuity of their corruption.

Since all the disbelievers were corrupters through disbelief, and some of them might sometimes act righteously in some of their deeds, he clarified that these were not like that, but were rather pure evil (sharr maḥḍ) (p-177). So he confirmed their exclusive devotion to corruption through his saying, explicitly stating what the form of the present tense had implied: ﴿and they did not reform﴾.

When the context called for a question about the explanation of some of their condition, he answered with His saying: ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by God"﴾. This is an imperative, from which the oath (qasam) is derived; that is, establish a mutual pledge and alliance among yourselves ﴿by God﴾, meaning the One who has no namesake, because of the widespread knowledge of His greatness and the all-encompassing reach of His knowledge and power. Let each of you then say on his own behalf and on behalf of those with him, as an indication that you are like one body: ﴿"That we will surely attack him"﴾, meaning Salih, ﴿"and his family"﴾, meaning that we will destroy all of them by night, for bayat (a night raid, from bayt) is the surprise attack on the enemy at night.

Since the custom is that those who carry out a night raid must leave some survivors behind, they said: ﴿"Then we will surely say to his heir"﴾, meaning the one who demands his blood if any of them survives: ﴿"We did not witness"﴾, meaning we were not present in full presence ﴿"the destruction"﴾, meaning the death ﴿"of his family"﴾, meaning the family of that heir, let alone that we would have carried it out; or the family of Salih, peace be upon him, let alone that we witnessed the destruction of Salih or carried out his killing, and there is no place for their destruction. Since the grief of his heir over the death of Salih, peace be upon him, was greater and more severe than the grief over the death of his family, the attribution of the matter to the heir in the context, on the assumption that the pronoun refers to Salih, peace be upon him, is the most complete guidance to the meaning, namely: "nor his destruction."

Since they had resolved upon this matter, and thought that they were exaggerating in swearing and boldly lying, they said: ﴿"And indeed we"﴾, meaning and we say within the oath, as an emphasis on the oath, giving the impression of the certainty of truthfulness: and indeed we ﴿"are truthful"﴾. How strange is a people who, when they bound themselves with oaths, resorted to God the Mighty, then fled from Him as the male ostrich flees, toward idols from which dry crushed herbage (hashim) is more beneficial.

Since this was the conduct of people who did not think that God knows what they do, the Exalted said, warning their like against such things: ﴿And they schemed a scheme﴾, i.e., they [concealed] a great concealment, intending by it evil [through this bargaining over the oath of sharing, so their scheme, which they strove to conceal, was for Us uncovered and in Our presence known and described; We perceived it, or rather We knew of it, and We nullified it]. ﴿And We schemed a scheme﴾ [i.e., We requited them for their deed with some of the greatness that is Ours], which is scheming in reality, for none of creation knows it. Therefore He said: ﴿while they perceive not﴾, i.e., despite their care in investigating matters and guarding against great decrees, no perception of what We had decreed against them ever arises in them in any way, let alone in others. This is because We made their destruction within their own planning, so they were unable to nullify it, and We placed them under the category of "kāna" (was), so not a single person of them escaped, and We destroyed all the disbelievers of their people in their dwellings (p-179) or outside their dwellings. As for their scheme, it was in their striving to perfect it and firmly arrange its affair, while they had permitted in it the safety of some of those they intended to destroy. Far apart are the two schemes, and very far is what lies between the two matters. It has become clear that the verse is either *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device of implicit mutual omission) or resembles it: the absence of perception indicates the omission of the absence of nullification from the second, and the omission of perception and of nullification, which is its result, from the first.

Since this vagueness (al-ibhām) signals the magnitude of the matter (tahwīl al-amr), Allah, glorified is He, made it the cause of an increase in that awe by saying: ﴿So look﴾, and He added greatness to it by indicating, through the interrogative particle, that it is worthy of being asked about, so He said: ﴿how was the outcome of their scheming﴾. For that is Our way (sunnatunā) with their likes. Then, to increase the awe, He resumed with an explanation of what had been left vague, saying: ﴿that We﴾, i.e., with the greatness that is ours. According to the reading of the one who opened the alif (anna), it is in his view a substitute (badal) for ﴿outcome﴾. ﴿We destroyed them﴾, i.e., We annihilated them, namely the nine who conspired together, by Our greatness, which has no like. ﴿And their people, all of them﴾: not one informant of them escaped, and there was no difference in that between the one who came forward and the one who turned back. And where could any of them, or any others apart from them, go beyond Our grip, or flee from Our dominion?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 52:

Since their destruction would naturally bring about increased terror and dread, (p-180) by pointing to their dwellings, in order to bring their conditions to mind and to magnify them through the greatness of their deeds, He said: ﴿So those are their houses﴾, i.e., those removed far away by the anger upon their people, ﴿ruined﴾, i.e., empty, collapsed and decayed, despite the strength of their pillars and the firmness of their construction. So glory be to the One who does what He wills, who is as capable of the weak as He is of the strong.

When He mentioned the destruction, He followed it with its cause in His saying: ﴿because they wronged﴾, i.e., they committed matters out of their proper places, like one walking in darkness, worshipping among the idols what deserves contempt and deserves no part of glorification in any way, turning away from the One whom they had none greater than at the time of swearing oaths, in times of hardship and anxiety, and (as Abu Hayyan said) the ruin of the houses and their emptiness of their people, so that none of them remained, which is the punishment the wrongdoers receive.

Then He increased the awe by His saying: ﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., the striking matter that is manifest to minds, which was done to Thamud, ﴿is surely a sign﴾, i.e., a great one, but it is ﴿for a people who know﴾, i.e., those who have knowledge. As for one who does not benefit from it, he has announced against himself that he is among the ranks of beasts.

Since that might have given the impression that destruction encompassed both groups, He said: ﴿And We saved﴾ by Our might ﴿those who believed﴾, or they [the group] who were with Salih, peace be upon him, all of them, ﴿and who were god-fearing﴾, i.e., characterized by taqwa (God-consciousness) to such a degree that it seemed they were naturally disposed to it, so they placed between themselves and what angers their Lord a shield (wiqaya) (p-181) of righteous deeds and profitable trades. And thus do We deal with everyone who does their deed. It was said: they were four thousand; Salih, peace be upon him, took them to Hadramawt, and when they entered it, Salih, peace be upon him, died, so it was named after that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 54:

When he finished the story of the close relative (al-qarib) who called his people, and they became two groups, after the strange case of the one who did not differ over him from among those he called, two (persons), he followed it with a strange case in which none from among those he called followed him, not a single person. He said, indicating that He, glory be to Him, has the choice: at times He makes affairs proceed according to analogy (qiyas), and at other times against the foundation (al-asas) that human intellects require. He said: ﴿And Lot﴾, meaning: And indeed We sent him. He pointed to the swiftness of his delivery with His words: ﴿when﴾, meaning: when ﴿he said to his people﴾, meaning: those among whom he had settled after he separated from his uncle Abraham the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, and had intermarried with them, and they used to commit the vile acts, rebuking and reproaching them: ﴿Do you commit the indecency﴾. Since the initial vagueness followed by specification has an effect of shaking and startling the soul that specification from the outset does not have, he said: ﴿the indecency﴾, meaning: the act most extreme in ugliness, ﴿while you see﴾, meaning: you have intellects by which you distinguish good from evil. It may be that some of them used to do it in the presence of others, as He said: ﴿and you commit the evil in your gatherings﴾ [al-Ankabut: 29], in which case it is then from sight (al-basar) and insight (al-basirah);

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 55:

Then he followed this denunciation with another denunciation of the content of a sentence emphasized with the utmost emphasis, to indicate that this act of theirs is one that the describer can hardly fully convey, and that no person of intellect would believe that anyone would commit it. So he specified what had been left vague, saying: ﴿Indeed, you approach men﴾, and he said "men" to draw attention to how far they are from what is proper for them to approach. Then he explained it by saying: ﴿with desire﴾, bringing them down to the rank of beasts, which have no intention of offspring nor any chastity. He said: ﴿instead of women﴾, meaning: approaching that begins from other than [the proper way], or [they are] at a lower rank than the rank of ﴿women﴾, indicating that they did wrong from both sides, in doing and in abstaining.

Since his saying ﴿with desire﴾ might have given the impression that they had no alternative to approaching them out of overpowering desire, but that women would not suffice for them, he negated this with his saying: ﴿Rather﴾, meaning: you do not approach them out of a desire that compels you, rather ﴿you are a people﴾. Since the aim of the surah is the manifestation of knowledge and wisdom, and they had opposed that either in deed or because they act with extravagance and other things like the conduct of the ignorant, he said: ﴿who act ignorantly﴾, meaning: you do this, openly displaying the adornment of desires, like those who are extreme in ignorance, who have no kind of knowledge, in openly committing vile acts out of corruption and in giving dominance to the characteristics of beasts, along with what Allah has provided you of intellects, which you have neglected until desire overcame them.

Al-Biqa'i indicated their extreme ignorance and their boasting about it, by what they built upon that in His saying: ﴿So there was not the answer of his people﴾, meaning: to this fine speech, since they had no proof to repel it, nor even a semblance of one, ﴿except that﴾ they confirmed his attribution of ignorance to them by ﴿saying﴾, turning to overpowering and persisting in wickedness: ﴿Expel the family of Lot﴾. So he made explicit what he had concealed in al-A'raf, because explicitness is more fitting to the subject of knowledge and wisdom and the disclosure of what is hidden. And they said, ﴿from your town﴾, as a favour bestowed upon him by allowing him to dwell among them. They justified this by their saying: ﴿Indeed they﴾ (and perhaps they expressed it with their saying ﴿people﴾, though the meaning is sound without it, as a mockery of him, since they understood from his words that he had lowered them to the rank of beasts) ﴿are men who keep themselves pure﴾, meaning: they consider our actions impure and hold themselves aloof from them.

When they had reached such a degree of depravity, He (Glory be to Him) attributed to their words and deeds the following: ﴿So We saved him and his family﴾, that is, all of them, from reaching him with harm or from any part of Our punishment befalling him, ﴿except his wife﴾. It is as if it were said: what became of her affair? It was said: ﴿We destined her﴾, that is, We decreed her, by Our greatness and power, in the judgment, even though she had gone out with him, ﴿to be among those who remained behind﴾, that is, those who remained in the town, in the reaching of their faces and the great calamity upon their own selves and their dwellings, until they became like yesterday's that had passed away.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 58:

﴿And We rained﴾. He indicated that it was a rain of punishment with stones, [although the verb is made transitive by the hamzah of ta'diyah (making a verb transitive), when it is already transitive without it, so it became as if it were for the removal of relief by bringing its opposite] by His saying: ﴿upon them﴾. He indicated the evil of the effect, because it entails the evil of the act from which it arose, and its strangeness, by His saying: ﴿a rain﴾, i.e., and what a rain! Therefore He made consequent upon it His saying: ﴿So evil was the rain of those who were warned﴾ (p-١٨٤) i.e., those to whom Our warning was given, the warning which is the warning.

When these stories were complete, the inference of what He, glory be to Him, intended from the proof of His wisdom, His knowledge, and His distinction from the idols in His power and forbearance was accomplished, He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to praise Him in thankfulness for what He had made known, and to make them acknowledge the impotence of their idols, refuting their ignorance by the clearest way and the nearest approach. So He said: ﴿Say﴾, which is the fruit of what preceded in this surah, namely ﴿Praise﴾, meaning the encompassing of the attributes of perfection, ﴿belongs to God﴾, meaning exclusively to the One who combines the most beautiful names and the highest attributes, both at the time of annihilation as at the time of origination, ﴿and peace﴾, meaning safety, well-being, and continuance in this time and in every time, as it was before this in the years gone by. By the particle of elevation in His saying ﴿upon﴾, He indicated that ruin cannot reach them. He indicated their nobility by His saying ﴿His servants﴾, by attributing them to Himself, and He confirmed this by His saying ﴿whom He has chosen﴾, meaning in every age and time, just as praise is due to their Worshipped One eternally and everlastingly, and not to those two (idols), and (He indicated) destruction and wrath upon whoever disobeyed, opposed the messengers and refused, as you see with the people of these reports. The meaning is that this constant judgment of the deliverance of the messengers and their followers, and the destruction of the disbelievers and their partisans, is a definitive proof that the encompassing belongs to God in every matter. Abu Hayyan said: This was the preface to what would be presented of the proofs indicating monotheism, knowledge, and power. Among what should be noticed is that in the story of Lot, peace be upon him, there is nothing beyond his prohibiting them from this abomination. So their situation is one of two matters: either they did not associate anything with God, the Exalted, but when they devised this predicament and openly persisted in it, they were seized with punishment for that and for their disbelief in denying their messenger, as the verse of the Poets explicitly states; or they were polytheists, but when he, peace be upon him, saw that they had sunk to the rank of beasts, he arranged his call for them from that to the rank of humanity, then to the rank of monotheism. The second estimation is indicated by His saying, pointing out that God, the Exalted, destroyed them and all who had disbelieved before them, and their deities did not avail them at all: ﴿Is God (not) better﴾, meaning the One who possesses majesty and honour, ﴿better﴾ for His servants whom He chose and so saved; ﴿or what they associate﴾, O company of Arabs, of idols and others, for their worshippers and lovers? For they cannot avail you at all, just as they did not avail those who worshipped them among these whom We destroyed, and you do not turn in fear during their calamities except to God alone. This is according to the recitation in the second person plural. The estimation according to the recitation in the third person, of the Basrans and ʿĀṣim, is: ﴿or what the disbelievers associate﴾, generally, anciently and recently, with those they associated with Him, so they were unable to benefit them when the calamity descended upon them. And the elative form (af‘al al-tafdil) is for silencing the opponent and drawing attention to the manifestness of his excessive error and his ignorance that leads him into ruin, to a degree that needs no uncovering of its outward aspect.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 60:

Since, along with this exposition, it is a clear matter that the implied sense is an increase in the rebuke of the polytheists and the affirmation of those who deny: "Who has done these acts, which are profound in wisdom and perfect in knowledge, or the one you have named a god, to whom there is no effect at all?" He returned to it with His saying: ﴿Or who﴾ (Amman). The original would have been "am huwa" (or is it He), but He expressed it with a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), whose original use is for one possessing knowledge, and joined it with what cannot be said of anything other than Him, so that it would be like a claim accompanied by proof. Thus He said: ﴿Created the heavens and the earth﴾, drawing attention, through the power to originate creation, to the power to restore it, and indeed a fortiori, as an indication of faith in the Hereafter, taking on the character of the believers, of whom it was stated at the beginning of the surah that this manifest Qur'an is good tidings for them.

Since growing plants is among the clearest signs of the reviving of the dead, He said: ﴿And sent down﴾ and increased their reproach, rebuke and censure with His saying: ﴿for you﴾, i.e., specifically for your sake, while you disbelieve in Him and attribute what He alone has done of that to others: ﴿water from the sky﴾, which is for the earth as the gushing water is for the wombs, as the water that will descend at the end of the ages upon the graves. (p-187) in its existence, its power, and its choosing to produce diverse things in taste, color, smell, nature and shape with one water in one earth, and His exclusive performance of that without any partner having any share of it at all. This is His greatest sign concerning the matter of resurrection. He turned to speaking [and] in the manner of majesty, and said: ﴿So We caused to grow﴾, i.e., by what We have of majesty, ﴿therewith gardens﴾, i.e., orchards enclosed, i.e., surrounded, by their trees and walls. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is everything of this kind, for it is in the sense that a wall could be built around it even if it has no wall. And from al-Farra', that an orchard which has no wall around it is not a garden (hadiqa).

Since the plural of multitude is more fitting for what does not reason, the description was given in the singular, indicating that they are like one thing in that description: ﴿of striking beauty﴾, i.e., splendor, goodliness, and radiance, and delight and joy in them, despite the closeness of their roots and the difference of their kinds, the variety of their tastes and shapes, their sizes and colors.

Since He affirmed the growing to Himself, He negated it from others in an emphatic manner, as an alert to the emphasis of His exclusive performance of it, and that if it is attributed to another, it is metaphorical, meaning causation, and that true agency belongs to Him alone. So He said: ﴿It was not for you﴾, i.e., it is not valid nor conceivable in any way ﴿to have﴾, while you are living, let alone your partners who are dead, rather inert, ﴿to cause its trees to grow﴾, i.e., the trees of (p-188) those gardens.

Since it has been established that He is alone in divinity, the denial and affirmation are well placed in His saying: ﴿Is there a god﴾, i.e., an existent one, ﴿with Allah﴾, i.e., the Supreme King who has no like.

Since the answer for every intelligent person is: No, by His might! He said, turning away from them to signify anger: ﴿Nay, but they﴾, i.e., in their calling upon a partner besides Him, glorified is He, ﴿are a people who deviate﴾, i.e., from the truth about which there is no doubt to something else, while knowing the truth, so they make others equal to Allah.

ولَمّا فَرَغَ مِن آيَةٍ اشْتَرَكَ فِيها الخافِقانِ، ذَكَرَ ما تَتَفَرَّدُ بِهِ الأرْضُ، لِأنَّها أقْرَبُ إلَيْهِمْ وهم بِحَقِيقَتِها وما بِسِواهُ مِن أحْوالِها أعْلَمُ مِنهم بِالأُمُورِ السَّماوِيَّةِ، تَعْدِيدًا لِلْبَراهِينِ الدّالَّةِ عَلى تَفَرُّدِهِ بِالفِعْلِ الدّالِّ عَلى تَفَرُّدِهِ بِالإلَهِيَّةِ (divinity)، فَقالَ مُبْدِلًا مِن ﴿أمَّنْ خَلَقَ﴾ [النمل: ٦٠] ﴿أمَّنْ﴾ أيْ: أمْ فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ الَّذِي ﴿جَعَلَ الأرْضَ قَرارًا﴾ أيْ: مُسْتَقِرَّةً في نَفْسِها لِيُقِرَّ عَلَيْها غَيْرَها، وكانَ القِياسُ يَقْتَضِي أنْ تَكُونَ هاوِيَةً أوْ مُضْطَرِبَةً كَما يَضْطَرِبُ ما هو مُعَلَّقٌ في الهَواءِ.

ولَمّا ذَكَرَ قَرارَها، أتْبَعَهُ دَلِيلَهُ في مَعْرِضِ الِامْتِنانِ فَقالَ: (p-١٨٩)﴿وجَعَلَ خِلالَها﴾ أيْ: في الأماكِنِ المُنْفَرِجَةِ بَيْنَ جِبالِها ﴿أنْهارًا﴾ أيْ: جارِيَةً عَلى حالَةٍ واحِدَةٍ، فَلَوِ اضْطَرَبَتِ الأرْضُ أدْنى اضْطِرابٍ، لَتَغَيَّرَتْ مَجارِي المِياهِ بِلا ارْتِيابٍ.

ولَمّا ذَكَرَ الدَّلِيلَ، ذَكَرَ سَبَبَ القَرارِ فَقالَ: ﴿وجَعَلَ لَها رَواسِيَ﴾ أيْ: كَمِراسِي السُّفُنِ، كانَتْ أسْبابًا في ثَباتِها عَلى مِيزانٍ دَبَّرَهُ سُبْحانَهُ في مَواضِعَ مِن أرْجائِها بِحَيْثُ اعْتَدَلَتْ جَمِيعُ جَوانِبِها فامْتَنَعَتْ مِنَ الِاضْطِرابِ.

ولَمّا أثْبَتَ القَرارَ وسَبَّبَهُ، وكانَ قَدْ جَعَلَ سُبْحانَهُ لِلْأنْهارِ طُرُقًا تَتَصَرَّفُ [فِيها] ولَوْ حَبَسَها عَنِ الجَرْيِ شَيْءٌ لَأوْشَكَ أنْ تَسْتَبْحِرَ، فَيَصِيرُ أكْثَرُ الأرْضِ لا يَنْتَفِعُ بِهِ في سَيْرٍ ولا نَباتٍ، أوْ أنْ تَخْرُقَ ذَلِكَ الحابِسُ بِما لَها مِن قُوَّةِ الجَرْيِ وشِدَّةِ النُّفُوذِ بِلَطافَةِ السَّرَيانِ، لِأنَّ مِن عادَةِ المِياهِ التَّخَلُّلَ بَيْنَ أطْباقِ التُّرابِ والتَّغَلْغُلَ بِما لَها مِنَ اللَّطافَةِ والرِّقَّةِ، والثِّقَلِ في الأعْماقِ ولَوْ قَلِيلًا قَلِيلًا، وكانَ سُبْحانَهُ قَدْ سَدَّ ما بَيْنَ البَحْرَيْنِ: الرُّومِيِّ والفارِسِيِّ، وكانَ ما بَيْنَهُما مِنَ الأرْضِ إنَّما هو يَسِيرٌ جِدًّا في بَعْضِ المَواضِعِ، وكانَ بَعْضُ مِياهِ الأرْضِ عَذْبًا، وبَعْضُهُ مِلْحًا، مَعَ (p-١٩٠)القُرْبِ جِدًّا مِن ذَلِكَ العَذْبِ، سَألَهم - تَنْبِيهًا لَهم عَلى عَظِيمِ القُدْرَةِ - عَنِ المُمْسِكِ لِعُدْوانِ أحَدِهِما عَلى آخَرَ، ولِعُدْوانِ كُلٍّ مِن خَلِيجَيِ المِلْحِ عَلى ما بَيْنَهُما لِئَلّا يَخْرُقاهُ فَيَتَّصِلا فَقالَ: ﴿وجَعَلَ بَيْنَ البَحْرَيْنِ حاجِزًا﴾ أيْ: يَمْنَعُ أحَدَهُما أنْ يَصِلَ إلى الآخَرِ.

ولَمّا كانَ مِنَ المَعْلُومِ أنَّهُ اللَّهُ وحْدَهُ لَيْسَ عِنْدَ عاقِلٍ شَكٌّ في ذَلِكَ، كَرَّرَ الإنْكارَ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿أإلَهٌ مَعَ اللَّهِ﴾ أيْ: المُحِيطِ عِلْمًا وقُدْرَةً، ولَمّا كانَ الجَوابُ الحَقُّ قَطْعًا: لا، وكانَ قَدْ أثْبَتَ لَهم في الإضْرابِ الأوَّلِ عِلْمًا مِن حَيْثُ الحُكْمُ عَلى المَجْمُوعِ، وكانَ كُلٌّ مِنهم يَدَّعِي رُجْحانَ العَقْلِ، وصَفاءَ الفِكْرِ، ورُسُوخَ القَدَمِ في العِلْمِ بِما يَدَّعِيهِ [العَرَبُ]، قالَ: ﴿بَلْ أكْثَرُهُمْ﴾ أيْ: الخَلْقُ الَّذِينَ يَنْتَفِعُونَ بِهَذِهِ المَنافِعِ ﴿لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ أيْ: لَيْسَ لَهم نَوْعٌ مِنَ العِلْمِ، بَلْ هم كالبَهائِمِ لِإعْراضِهِمْ عَنْ هَذا الدَّلِيلِ الواضِحِ.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 62:

When He had guided them by the signs of the horizons, and all of these were among the states of ease, and they were in a position of heedlessness of God (al-Ilah), He reminded them of what is in their own selves, which the change of states requires, the states that by their very nature point to God, and which call every intelligent person to sincerity of direction toward Him, sincerity of intention before Him, and turning to Him. Upon this the natural dispositions are fixed, and the consensus has been established, so there is no dispute concerning it. So He said: ﴿Is He who answers the one in distress﴾, meaning: the category of the one who seeks refuge in what has no power over him, [a refuge] that is able, for the few and the many alike, to answer when He wills, as you witness. He expressed this and what follows with the present tense because it is something that renews itself, unlike what came before concerning the creation of the heavens, and what follows it. ﴿When he calls upon Him﴾, meaning: when harm makes you forget your partners, and drives you to the One who created you, and distracts the one who denies (the divine attributes) from his doctrine, and makes him heedless of his bad manners, through the great intensity of his turning to the fulfilment of his need.

Since answering has two sides, bringing joy and repelling harm, and consideration of the second is more intense, He singled it out first, saying: ﴿and removes the evil﴾. Then He followed it with the first in a more general form, saying, pointing to the great favour upon them in making them empowered and exalted over all who are on the earth and what is in the earth, honoured by His vicegerency, glory be to Him, and for this reason He turned to them: 

﴿and makes you successors of the earth﴾, meaning: in that some of you succeed others. He continually renews this by destroying one generation and bringing forth another until the Hour. And since this is clearer, He repeated the rebuke concerning it, reproaching them for forgetfulness, saying: ﴿Is there a god﴾, meaning: existing or present ﴿with Allah﴾, meaning: the Supreme King, to whom there is no equal.

Then He resumed the rebuke, to make it grave and to confront them with it, in the recitation of the majority (the reading with the second person), because the lifting of these calamities implies nearness, which calls for direct address. For this reason He emphasised it by adding "mā", saying: ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾, meaning: that He who saved you from that alone, when you sincerely turned to Him at the intensifying of the matter, is the Owner of all your affairs in ease just as He was the Owner of them in hardship; and that the idols possess nothing, by intercession or otherwise, just as they did not possess anything in your belief at times of crisis and the intensifying of distresses, in great matters. For this is an evident analogy and a striking proof. But it is in human nature to forget the harm they were in when good comes. As for the one who read with the yā' (the third person, "yatadhakkarūn"), namely Abū 'Amr, Hishām and Rawḥ, it signifies anger, which is most fitting toward disbelief, together with the great benefaction.

When He had mentioned the signs of the earth and concluded with the one in distress (al-mudtarr), and since the one in distress may not find the way to any means of escape, He followed them with the signs of the heavens, mentioning what is among the greatest forms of distress, and said: ﴿Who guides you﴾, meaning: when you travel, by the landmarks He has set for you, both the heavenly and the earthly ones, ﴿in the darknesses of the land﴾, meaning: by the stars, the mountains, and the winds. Although these are the weakest of the guides, one may be driven to them where none of those two appears (p-193) ﴿and of the sea﴾, by the stars and the winds.

Since the winds are, as they are, among the indicators of travel, and some of them are among the indicators of rain, He said: ﴿And who sends the winds﴾, meaning those which are among the indicators of travel, ﴿as heralds﴾ [al-Mursalat: 3], meaning they spread the clouds and gather them ﴿before His mercy﴾, meaning the rain, calling the cause by the name of its effect. The winds by which one is guided in one's directions are four: al-Saba, al-Dabur, al-Shamal, and al-Janub, and they are the weakest of the indicators. The Imam Abu Hilal al-Hasan ibn Abd Allah al-Askari said in his book Asma' al-Ashya' wa Sifatiha: "The winds are four: al-Shamal, which comes on your right when you face the qiblah of Iraq, meaning the area between the summer rising points of the sun and the Bana Na'sh (the Great Bear stars). In summer it is hot, and its name is al-Barih. Al-Janub is opposite to it. Al-Saba comes from the rising of the sun and is al-Qabul, and al-Dabur is opposite to it. It is also said that al-Janub is al-Nu'amā and al-Arnab." End of quotation.

This expression is the clearest of the expressions in identifying these winds. The Imam Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Abi Ahmad ibn al-Qass (p-194) al-Tabari al-Shafi'i said in his book Adillat al-Qiblah: "The qiblah of the Iraqis is toward the whole door of the Ka'bah, up to the Syrian corner which is near the Black Stone." He said: "The people of knowledge have differed greatly regarding this matter, that is, in describing the locations of the winds. The closest of these, according to what I have tested and observed in Makkah, is that al-Saba blows between the rising points of the sun in winter and the rising of Suhayl (Canopus). Suhayl's setting place, by apparent observation, is over the roof of the Ka'bah when it rises." Sahib al-Qamus said: "Al-Saba is a wind whose direction is from the rising of the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) to the Bana Na'sh." He said: "Al-Qabul, like Sabur, is the wind of al-Saba, because it faces al-Dabur, or because it faces the door of the Ka'bah, or because the soul turns it over."

The Imam Abu Abd Allah al-Qazzaz said: "Al-Saba is the wind that blows from the rising of the sun, and al-Qabul is the wind that blows from the rising of the sun, because it faces al-Dabur. It is also said that it is so because it faces the door of the Ka'bah, and that is al-Saba." Thus their statements, as you see, agree against Ibn al-Qass. Ibn al-Qass said: "It (al-Saba) is a wind that carries comfort, lightness, and gentle breeze, blowing from between the eastern point of winter and the rising of Suhayl. (p-195) Its cold bites more sharply than its blowing. It fertilizes the trees, and it blows only at night. Its dominion is when night darkens, until day brightens and the sun rises. It is at its strongest in the hours before dawn, between the two dawns. Al-Janub blows between the rising of Suhayl and the setting of the sun in summer."

Sahib al-Qamus said: "Al-Janub is a wind that opposes al-Shamal, its direction is from the rising of Suhayl to the rising of the Pleiades." And from Ibn Hisham al-Lakhmi: al-Janub is the qiblah wind. In the combination of al-Ubab and al-Muhkam: "Al-Janub is a wind that opposes al-Shamal, coming from the right of the qiblah." It was also said: "Among the winds, it is the one that meets you on your left when you stand facing the qiblah." Ibn al-A'rabi said: "The direction of al-Janub is from the rising of Suhayl to the rising of the Pleiades." Al-Asma'i said: "When al-Janub comes, good and fertilization come with it, and when al-Shamal comes, it dries things out. It is said of two people who are on good terms: their wind is al-Janub, and when they separate it is said: their wind has become al-Shamal." From Ibn al-A'rabi: "Al-Janub is hot everywhere except in Najd, where it is cold." (p-196) Ibn al-Qass said: "When it blows, its strength is greater in the height and in the air, because it is charged with the clouds, moving the branches and the tops of the trees. Despite that, you see it gathering the clouds in the sky, and you see them piled up and laden." He said: "I heard someone say: 'Whenever its blowing intensifies, rain is feared, and whenever al-Janub blows and is followed by al-Dabur, rain falls. It stirs up the sea and brings out every full dew on the earth, and it is from the wind of Paradise.'"

Al-Dabur: Sahib al-Qamus said: "It is a wind opposite to al-Saba." Al-Qazzaz said: "It is the one that comes from behind the Ka'bah, and it is the one that faces the rising of the sun." Ibn al-Qass said: "It blows between the setting points of the sun in summer and the rising of the Bana Na'sh. Its strength on the earth is greater than its strength in the air. When it blows, it raises dust, sweeps the ground, lifts the skirts, and strikes the feet. It raises dust most when it deviates, so you see it as if it were being sprinkled with dirt over the face of the earth. In the wilderness and sands, you see the trees humming from the direction of al-Dabur, the dust gathered at their roots, and what lies to the south bare, exposed, and eager." Its strength on the earth, and God knows best, is because 'Ad were threatened with destruction by wind. They dug pits and hid in them, so God sent al-Dabur, which entered the pits and cast them out, destroyed and annihilated, until it had consumed them.

Al-Shamal: Sahib al-Qamus said: "It is the wind that blows from the direction of the Black Stone." The correct view is that its direction is between the setting of the sun and the Bana Na'sh, or from the rising of the Bier (al-Na'sh) to the setting of the Flying Eagle (al-Nasr al-Ta'ir) (p-197), and it hardly blows at night.

Al-Qazzaz said: "It is the wind that comes on your left when you face the rising of the sun. The Arabs say: 'al-Janub said to al-Shamal: I have a merit over you, for I travel at night and you do not travel at night.' Al-Shamal replied: 'The free woman does not travel at night.'" Al-Saghani said in Majma' al-Bahrayn: "Al-Shamal is the wind that blows from the direction of the pole." From Abu Hanifa: "It is the one that blows from the direction of the northern pole, and it is al-Jirbiya'. It is also the Syrian wind, because it comes to them from the side of Syria." In the combination of al-Ubab and al-Muhkam: "Al-Bawarih: the severity of winds from the north in summer, not in winter, as if it were the plural of barihah. It was said: al-Bawarih are the severe winds that carry dust, singular barih." Al-Jirbiya' is the wind between al-Janub and al-Saba. It was said: it is the nakba' (an intermediate wind) that runs between al-Shamal and al-Dabur. It is a wind that disperses clouds. It was also said: it is al-Shamal, and its jirbiya' is its coldness, as al-Asma'i said. Al-Layth said: "It is the cold al-Shamal." Ibn al-Qass said: "Al-Shamal blows from between the rising of the Bier and the rising of the sun in winter. It cuts through the cloud and erases it, and for this reason al-Shamal is called al-Mahwah (the eraser). He said: 'This is the case in the land of the Hijaz. As for the land of Iraq and the East, the al-Janub often drives a cloud and gathers it without milking it, until al-Shamal blows and milks it. Al-Janub and al-Shamal are alike, because both are charged with the clouds: al-Janub drives them when they are laden (p-198), and al-Shamal turns them back and erases them when they have poured out.'" Abu Ubayda said: "For the Arabs, al-Shamal is for refreshment, al-Janub is for rains and dew, al-Dabur is for calamity, the mildest of which is a violent dust that blinds the eyes, and al-Saba is for the fertilizing of trees. Every wind of these winds that veers and falls between two winds is a nakba', and it is called so because it deviates from the direction of the four mentioned above." End of quotation.

Al-Mas'udi said in Muruj al-Dhahab, in mentioning the nomadic people and the reason for choosing the desert: "A certain orator of the Arabs came to Kisra and asked him about various things, including the winds. He said: 'From between Suhayl to the edge of the whiteness of dawn is al-Janub. What is opposite them, coming from the west, is al-Shamal. What comes from behind the Ka'bah is al-Dabur, and what comes from before it is al-Saba.'"

Ibn Kathir, in Surat al-Nur, quoted from Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir, from Ubayd ibn Umayr al-Laythi, that he said: "God sends al-Muthirah, which sweeps the earth clean; then God sends al-Nashi'ah, which creates the clouds; then God sends al-Mu'allifah, which gathers them together; then God sends al-Lawaqih, which fertilize the clouds."

When what has been previously mentioned of the signs had revealed what they were in the darkness of weak doubts, and the proofs became clear, and no excuse remained for anyone in any of these matters, He, glorified is He, repeated the denunciation in His saying: ﴿Is there a god with God?﴾, meaning: the One whose knowledge is perfect, so that His power encompasses all things.

(p-199) When He had mentioned the state of distress and followed it with forms of it, including the darkness of the sea, and they used to sincerely devote themselves to Him, glorified is He, while at sea, abandoning their associates, He alerted them that this necessitates believing that sincerity to Him is obligatory at all times. He followed this with His saying, as a matter of magnification, turning away from them with the consensus of the ten (readers), in the manner of one whose anger has reached its height: ﴿Exalted is God﴾, meaning the Doer, the Capable, the Chooser, who has no equal, ﴿above what they associate with Him﴾, meaning: for none of these has any power over anything of that, and how can the rank of incapacity compare with the rank of power?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 64:

When Allah, glorified is He, arranged these proofs in this manner, ascending from the more general to the more specific, and from the earth to the heavens, He concluded them with that which encompasses them and other things, as guidance toward analogizing what is unseen from them to what is witnessed. Thus there necessarily follows, with certainty, the power to bring back (creation). So He drove them toward that in the manner of something witnessed and accepted, and He counted those who denied it among those who are not to be given attention. [So He said:] ﴿Or who originates creation﴾, meaning all of it: what you know of it and what you do not know. Then ﴿He brings it back﴾, because every thing is perishing except His Face. This attribute, by your acknowledgment, is continually renewed in its relation (to Him). Since it is a clear necessity for them to affirm the return, because they admit that whoever brings something into being is able to bring it back, for the return is easier, He said: ﴿Then He brings it back﴾, meaning: after He annihilates it.

Since rain and the growth of plants are among the clearest indications of the return, He said, referring to them in a manner that covers all that has passed: ﴿And who provides for you from the heaven﴾, meaning by rain, heat, cold and other things that have a cause in forming or coloring (the world), ﴿and the earth﴾, meaning by plants, minerals, animals and other things that none knows except Allah. He expressed these as "provision" because through it is the completion of blessing. ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, meaning: the one who possesses the attributes of majesty and honor, existing, or doing any of those things?

Since all of these are clear proofs, manifest evidences, shining lights, dazzling arguments, plain proofs and overpowering authorities, establishing the Oneness (of Allah), which necessitates the power to resurrect and everything else possible, He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was commanded to turn away from them, signaling (divine) anger at their end, [by ordering them] to bring a single proof for the soundness of their belief. So He said: ﴿Say﴾, meaning: these claimants to reason, ﴿Bring your proof﴾, meaning: for denying any of that to Allah, the Exalted, or for affirming any of it to another, so that the claim of partnership in creation would be established, and then they would hear the claim of partnership in divinity. Let your bringing of that be immediate without delay, because whoever claims reason cannot accomplish anything except with a present proof. ﴿If you are truthful﴾, meaning: in your claim that you are right that there is something other than Allah with Allah. He ascribed the proof to them in a form that suggests stubbornness, as though there were no dispute about its existence and realization; the intent is to bring it, all of this as mockery of them and as an alert that they went far astray into error and sank deep into the impossible, in that they were content for themselves with a religion to which no intelligent person would turn except after attaining certainty of its soundness, and there is no doubt that they have no basis for any of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 65:

Since the contents of these proofs depend on knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb), for the hidden thing (al-khabʾ) is not brought forth by the origination of creation, the removal of harm, or the perfect arrangement of affairs except through it, because there is no power at all for one who has no knowledge, and no perfection of power for one who lacks perfect knowledge, as its explanation has passed in Ta-Ha, and since He, glorified be He, at the end of these proofs challenged them to produce a proof for polytheism, and they would sometimes say, "We will bring it," He commanded that they know that there is no proof for them regarding it, rather the proof stands against it. So He said: ﴿Say﴾, that is, to them, or to everyone who claims their claim: ﴿None knows﴾ [anyone], but He expressed it with the particle for rational beings, saying ﴿whoever﴾, so that a disputatious person would not restrict it to what does not reason. He expressed it with the adverbial form (al-zarf) to alert that the thing contained is hidden, and every container (zarf) is a barrier for what it contains from knowing what is beyond it. So He said: ﴿in the heavens and the earth the unseen﴾, that is, the utterly unseen, which has not come out into the world of witnessing (al-shahadah) at all, and no sign points to it, so that they could be capable of anything of what has preceded in these verses of matters, and thus know it.

Since God, exalted be He, is exempt from being contained by any place, the exception here is made disjunctive (munqati'), and the disjunctive exception by rights takes the accusative [as Ibn Abi Ablah read it, an anomalous reading], but it was read in the nominative [by the consensus of the ten readers] as a substitute (badal) according to the dialect of [the tribe of] Tamim. It was said: (p-202) ﴿except Allah﴾, that is, the One specially characterized by the attributes of perfection, as is said in the poetry:

A land in which there is no companion except the gazelles and except the camels

meaning: if the gazelles are companions, then there is a companion in it, a decisive affirmation against the claim that it is empty of companions. So the meaning of the verse becomes: if God, may He be exalted, is among those in the heavens and the earth, then among them there is one who knows the unseen; that is, the knowledge of any one of them of the unseen is as impossible as it is impossible that God be among them. It is also valid that it be a connected exception. The adverbial sense in relation to Him, glorified be He, is a metaphor with respect to His knowledge, though it contains a combination of the literal and the metaphorical. On this basis it is raised as a substitute or as a qualifier, and the nominative is more eloquent than the accusative, because it follows a negated statement. By this the secret of His not saying "None knows the unseen except Him" becomes known, and that is the alerting to the state of being contained and to need, and that the container is a barrier, about which no doubter doubts. Ibn Malik made the dependent element of the adverbial phrase specific, estimating it as "is mentioned"; others made "whoever" the object and "the unseen" a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), and the exception an emptied one (mufarragh), so the estimate becomes: none knows the unseen of those mentioned — that is, what is absent from them — all of them, except Him.

Since the report that no one among people has been informed of may be told by soothsayers (al-kuhhan), or by someone of the jinn, from the hollows of idols, and they used to call this "unseen" although in reality it is not so, because they heard it from the heaven after God had made it manifest to the angels and whomever of His servants He wills, and since they would sometimes evade with it from the expression, and the Hour had been established as a matter and the mention of it had spread in the Qur'an and on the tongues of the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, and their companions, may God be pleased with them, to the point that it became like something beyond dispute, and the knowledge of its time was purely of the unseen, He said: ﴿and they do not perceive﴾, that is, none of those in the heavens and the earth, even if they gather and cooperate, ﴿when﴾ [that is:] at what time ﴿they will be raised﴾. So whoever knows anything of that with certainty, his truthfulness becomes evident, and whoever conjectures, his falsehood becomes evident.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 66:

When the Prophet (ﷺ) had been sent while disbelief had spread over the earth, and they had greatly insisted on denying the Hour and had firmly rejected it, some explicitly and some by implication, because of their straying from the path of the messengers, and it was fitting for the wise scholar not to be certain of anything until his knowledge of it was complete, He said, mocking them, as you say to the most ignorant of people, "How knowledgeable you are!", ridiculing them. He added, to negate their awareness of it and to show their lie through the confusion of their speech: ﴿Rather, their knowledge has come to completion﴾, meaning it has reached its limit and ended, ﴿concerning the Hereafter﴾, meaning concerning its affair in general: the knowledge of its time and the measure of its greatness, what it is, and other descriptions of it. This is because they were certain in denying it, and they colluded (p-204) in that, and varied their expressions about it, and elaborated their talk on this matter. This is the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, and likewise the reading of the rest, ادّارَكَ (idarraka), meaning تَدارَكَ (tadarraka), that is, it followed in succession and became firmly established.

Since they, despite their explicit certainty in denying it, were lying in their certainty and confused in their ignorance, and since they sometimes express it as doubt, which is a sign that they have no knowledge of it, He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt﴾. Since, because of the intensity of its evidence and the strength of its proofs, it is as if it were already existent, He used مِن (min), meaning "beginning from": ﴿concerning it﴾. Since they would at times affirm its negation with certainty and at other times waver, the true state of one who denies a thing, sometimes with certainty and sometimes with doubt, is to be described with extreme ignorance of it. So He said: ﴿Rather, they are﴾ [blind]. Since man is naturally disposed to shortcomings that cause his transgression and his exaggeration of exaltedness in all his affairs, and only the fear of being presented before his Lord weakens those shortcomings in him, which fear would end his ignorance and his persistence in his ugly deeds, He said, placing the prepositional phrase first: ﴿concerning it, blind﴾. Meaning: their extreme and established blindness began from their confusion regarding it. They went astray, and their straying blinded them to everything that would benefit them, so they no longer benefited from their intellects; rather, their benefit was reversed into harm and their good into evil. He attributed what was mentioned to all who are in the heavens and the earth, because the action of some may be attributed to all for a purpose, and the purpose here is to alert to the greatness of this matter and the extremity of its description, and that everyone must give it attention, stand by its due, and refrain from its falsehood. [Or, it is attributed because some doubt while the rest remain silent, for the purpose of magnifying it. Or, the attainment of knowledge in terms of the magnification is through the establishment of proofs, which are clearer than the sun, so they are, with respect to them, in the position of one who has grasped the knowledge of a thing yet turns away from it, having forfeited for himself the good whose reality he does not know. Then he descended a further step through doubt, then destroyed it entirely, and blindness lowered him to the rank of the beasts, whose only concern is the pleasure of the belly and the genitals. This is like one who hears of the difference among the schools of thought and of some of them misguiding others, and so he misguides some of them without examining what they say, and becomes one who gropes like a blind camel, and whose affair against his opponent is trivial.] Or, it is doubt, because their actions are the actions of one in doubt. Or, because they lack knowledge of the exact time, they are as if in doubt, rather, in blindness. Also, because intellects and sciences cannot independently grasp anything of its affair, and it is taken only from God through His messengers, from the angels and from humans, and whoever takes any of its knowledge from other than them [goes astray].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 27, verse 67:

Since the implied sense was to relay their speech, which indicates that knowledge had reached them, so they said, swearing by the utmost of their oaths: ﴿The Hour will not come upon us,﴾ he (Allah) joined to it what indicates doubt and blindness. The original form would have been "and they said," but He said: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾ [i.e., they concealed (sataru) the proofs of the Oneness (of God) and of the Hereafter, which are too numerous to be counted and clearer than daylight], attaching the judgment to the description, while they put forward questions in the manner of one who deems it far-fetched and denies it: ﴿When we have become dust, and our fathers, shall we really be brought forth?﴾ They repeated the interrogation (p-206), as a sign of the extreme of their far-fetching and denial, and they counted what they deemed far-fetched to be impossible. So they said: ﴿Shall we really﴾ i.e., we and our fathers, whose time has been long and in whom decay has taken firm hold, ﴿be brought forth﴾ i.e., from the state we have come to, of death and decay, back to what we were before that, of life and strength.

Then they set forth their proof, in their own assumption, for this, and they said, giving a reason for their disbelief in it: ﴿Indeed we were promised this﴾

Since the concern in this surah is with firm certainty in the Hereafter, he (the speaker) placed the words ﴿this﴾, meaning the bringing out from the graves, ﴿as we were the first time﴾ before ﴿we and our fathers﴾, unlike what preceded in Surah al-Mu'minun. They also said ﴿before﴾ as an increase in their disbelief, meaning: ages have passed over this promise and nothing has come of it from Him, and this is therefore evidence that it has no reality. It is as if it were said: then what is meant by it? So they said: ﴿it is not﴾, meaning: this is nothing but ﴿the fables of the ancients﴾, meaning: what they inscribed as falsehood for a matter whose intended meaning we do not know, and whose meaning has no reality. Thus their speech, as you see, has descended to this level, and on the other hand they are at times in the extreme of denial, like one who claims to encompass knowledge, and at times they seek to deem it improbable, like the doubter whose ignorance is compounded, deserving of mockery, as has passed, that this is the meaning of the successive turns (idrabat) — and God is the Granter of success.

(p-207) When there remained, after this proof of His power over everything in general and over the Resurrection in particular, no statement that could turn them back from error except the threat of punishment, and when their speech was causing the Prophet ﷺ such grief and distress as only Allah the Exalted knows, He, glorified is He, addressed him, instructing him and guiding them in the form of a threat, saying: ﴿Say: Travel through the land﴾, meaning: O you who are obstinate, or blind and ignorant.

Since the intent is to seek guidance toward belief and a return from error and obstinacy, given that the context calls for this and not mere threat, He said ﴿then look﴾, with the fa' (fa, "then") that implies haste, and He magnified the matter to be observed by making it worthy of care and of inquiry about it. So He said: ﴿how was﴾, meaning, as a state of utmost possibility, ﴿the end of the criminals﴾, meaning those who severed what Allah commanded to be joined: from the prayer, which is the connection between Allah and His servants, and from the zakat, which is a connection between some servants and others, because they denied the messengers, who are the guides to that which the intellects cannot independently grasp. So they denied the Hereafter, belief in which produces every guidance and denial of which produces every blindness, as the indication to this was already mentioned at the beginning of the surah. For if you look at their dwellings and reflect upon their histories with true reflection, that would hasten you toward belief, and you would be saved; otherwise you would perish, and you would harm only yourselves. A further explanation of this has already preceded in Surat al-Nahl. (p-208)

When the Prophet (ﷺ) was seized by grief, because of their coarseness in their blindness to the path to which the Guide had led, a grief that only God knows, He said: ﴿Do not grieve over them﴾, that is, over their failure to believe.

Since they did not limit themselves to denial, but also sought to bring harm upon the believers and set snares for them, He said: ﴿And do not be﴾, retaining the *nun* (the final consonant of the verb, the nūn), because the context is one of reporting their obstinacy and mockery, together with the sufficiency of God, glorified and exalted, against their scheming through the evil punishment He has prepared for them in both abodes. There is therefore no call for the utmost concision and emphasis in negating distress [so that the retained *nun* conveys firmness, and he is not forbidden from what the hardship cannot be separated from, which is indicated by God's words: ﴿We know that your breast is distressed by what they say﴾ (al-Hijr 15:97), and He only forbids persistence with them in mention]. This differs from what passed in al-Nahl, for the context there concerns justice in punishment, because of the calamity that befell them at the Battle of Uhud. That calls for greatly magnifying consolation by urging patience, and negating [all] distress, so that this would restrain from exceeding the limit, and rather move toward pardon. ﴿In distress﴾, that is, in the breast, ﴿over what they scheme﴾. For God makes their destruction lie in their own plotting, like the tyrants of the people of Ṣāliḥ.

(p-209) When he had indicated that they had left no way open for exaggeration in denying the Hour, he indicated that in threatening them with the Hour and with other punishments of Allah they were even more extreme. So He said: ﴿And they say﴾, with the present tense that signals renewal at every moment, indicating continuity: ﴿When is this promise?﴾ They called it a "promise" to show affection, mockingly, while meaning punishment, resurrection and recompense. ﴿If you are﴾, that is, you and whoever follows you, in a state that is firmly established, ﴿truthful, as you claim﴾.

Al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar, on Surah 27, verse 72:

He answered them, with respect to this stammering reply, with the reply of the Vast, the Able, who is not beset by constraint and whom haste does not overtake, indicating readiness either for defense or for submission to the One of Majesty and Honor, as Bilqis, may Allah be pleased with her, did. He then addressed the one (i.e., the Prophet) who, other than Him, cannot truly attain this deliberateness, saying: ﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿perhaps﴾, i.e., it is possible, ﴿it will be that﴾, and it is fitting and appropriate that it be, ﴿there has followed﴾, i.e., followed closely (radf), until it became like the rider behind (al-radif) and caught up.

Since the verb was made intransitive and was given the sense of what is transitive with the lam, for the sake of restriction, he said: ﴿for you﴾, i.e., for your sake specifically, ﴿some of what you are hastening﴾, its coming, of the threat, so that you seek to hasten it before the time Allah set for it. So, upon its occurrence, what have you prepared to repel it? For the intelligent person is one who looks into the consequences of his affairs and builds them upon the worst assumptions, so he prepares for what he imagines of calamity that which will be for him (p-210) a means of deliverance, as Bilqis, may Allah be pleased with her, did by submitting, which brings safety, since what prevailed upon her thought was that refusal entails humiliation; not as the people of Salih did with the caves, which aided in their destruction, and others of the Pharaohs.

Since the implied meaning was definite, namely, "Indeed your Lord does not hasten to punish the people of sin with retribution, despite the certainty of His complete power," he followed it with His words: ﴿And indeed your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is gracious to you by being forbearing toward your community and by not hastening punishment upon them for their sins, ﴿is truly full of bounty﴾, that is, of bestowing favor and grace, ﴿upon mankind﴾, that is, all of them, ﴿but most of them do not give thanks﴾, that is, they do not render thanks to Him for the blessings He has bestowed [upon them, and they increase in ignorance through their haste].
